RECORD-00757.quote: Suppose that getting the separations right isn't the central problem. This is what public journalism is saying: getting the connections right is the deeper challenge in journalism right now.
RECORD-00757.author: Sarah Darville

CLIP-00040.summary: Article discusses the definition of journalists and their rights in the context of citizen journalism and blogger protections. Mentions Jay Rosen of NYU's journalism program in the context of discussing citizen journalism and how it relates to traditional journalism.
CLIP-00040.quote: The rise of citizen journalism and bloggers forces a reckoning with who counts as a journalist and what legal protections should follow from that status.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
CLIP-00040.author: The Griffin Daily News

TUMBLR-00120.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20 gets an assignment from Quartz News These specs were sent by the editors of Quartz to Professor Jay Rosen as part of Studio 20’s networked reporting project in spring 2013. Jay Rosen responded with his presentation, Designs for a Networked Beat , May 13, 2013. The problem: As well as Quartz’s longer-term obsessions, we often obsess on shorter-term stories that turn into big news for a few days or weeks, but that we don’t know in advance are going to become big.
TUMBLR-00120.quote: Quartz editors identified a key editorial challenge: stories that turn into big news for days or weeks often cannot be identified in advance as significant, making networked beat reporting difficult to plan.
TUMBLR-00120.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00121.summary: We had six partners: ProPublica, The Wall Street Journal Social Media Desk, Mashable.com’s gaming beat, PandoDaily.com, Fast Company and Quartz News (qz.com). Each came to class and explained  the problems they have making more productive use of a networked approach. The Wall Street Journal Social Media desk A tool for locating likely sources within an established Twitter network.
TUMBLR-00121.quote: Studio 20's networked reporting project partnered with six news organizations—including ProPublica, The Wall Street Journal Social Media Desk, and Quartz—to explore how journalism can make more productive use of a networked approach.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00121.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00755.summary: Joshua Benton interviews Rosen for the Nieman Lab Press Publish podcast, covering his entry into journalism academia, the influence of James Carey and Neil Postman, the Lippmann-Dewey debate, the rise and quasi-fall of civic journalism, why horse race journalism needs improvement, and what Rosen calls 'the production of innocence' -- journalism's way of distancing itself from its own role in political outcomes.
RECORD-00755.quote: Jay has been so valuable to the field -- he's an inside-outside voice pricking journalism when it needs to be pricked. His ideas, once shouted down in newsrooms, have become something closer to received wisdom for many.
RECORD-00755.author: Joshua Benton

TUMBLR-00098.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20 would like to extend a big thanks to everyone who made it out for last night’s Open Studio presentations and helped make the night a big success! You can find more info on the ten innovative presentations below: Kat Patke: User-to-User Community Building with the Huffington Post Laura Edwins: Decoding User Engagement with the Christian Science Monitor Silva Shih: Data Viz On The Go with Quartz Nadja Popovich: Re-framing elections with the Guardian US Khwezi Magwaza and Patrice Peck: PUSH New Media: Collaborative Innovation (with test partner Ebony.com) Yoo Eun Lee: Video Template with Global Voices Tracy Levy: Online Video: How What Why with Tablet Tando Ntunja: Clients-As-Storytellers/Clients-As-Reporters with Safe Horizons ATP Ana Maria Benedetti: Dreamers Across America with UNIVISION 0 notes
TUMBLR-00098.quote: Studio 20's Open Studio showcased ten innovative student projects spanning user engagement, data visualization, election framing, and collaborative media partnerships.
TUMBLR-00098.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00094.summary: PUSH worked with Ebony.com as a test client to develop an original man-on-the-street video series, among other creative multimedia projects. The new template will encourage contributors to package existing content (text and images) into video news clips. She has been working on funding, design and community outreach, including advisory sessions with Homicide Watch.
TUMBLR-00094.quote: Studio 20 projects like PUSH developed original multimedia series for real clients such as Ebony.com, with students working on video production, community outreach, and funding alongside editorial work.
TUMBLR-00094.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00086.summary: ¶ ● Lewis Dvorkin fields some good questions from Studio 20 Lewis Dvorkin recently stopped in Studio 20 to talk with first year masters students about innovation in the digital age. “We felt like equals, which is really cool when you’re talking to the head honcho of online media at Forbes,” notes Studio-20er Simran Khosla . Well, it’s far more than making phone calls, writing a story and going home.
TUMBLR-00086.quote: Journalism today is far more than making phone calls, writing a story and going home.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00086.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00063.summary: Rosen analyzes the dynamics between presidential campaigns, the Commission on Presidential Debates, and journalists moderating debates. It highlights the tension between the desire of campaigns to control the debate format and the journalist's role in pressing for answers and holding candidates accountable. Rosen explores different moderator styles, from the 'Vanishing Moderator' to a more active interlocutor, and argues that the lack of consensus on the ideal approach reflects a deeper question about whether presidential power needs an independent check.
RECORD-00063.quote: The debates in their current form are a temporary alliance among three players: the campaigns of the major-party candidates for president, the Commission on Presidential Debates and the journalists who are chosen to moderate and maintain order.
RECORD-00063.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00084.summary: Working with a media partner, they each have to design and execute their own project in innovation. Laura Edwins is partnering with The Christian Science Monitor in Boston to build a user engagement strategy for their politics blog, DC Decoder . The new template will encourage contributors to package existing contents (text and image) into video news clips.
TUMBLR-00084.quote: Studio 20 students each designed and executed their own incremental innovation project in partnership with a real media outlet, translating journalism theory into working prototypes with actual editorial partners.
TUMBLR-00084.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00082.summary: ¶ ● The skills Studio 20 students have and want to gain Jay Rosen asked the incoming class of Studio 20 students to participate in an inventory: the skills they came in with and the skills they most wanted to acquire during their 16-month graduate program. Then they had to come up with a way of representing it that tapped into some of those skills, plus they had to introduce themselves and their backgrounds. (Asked what the takeaway was, the students said: next time, don’t build it in flash!)
TUMBLR-00082.quote: Jay Rosen asked incoming Studio 20 students to inventory the skills they arrived with and the ones they most wanted to acquire during their 16-month graduate program, then represent that data in a format that drew on those very skills.
TUMBLR-00082.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00081.summary: That’s when I got a job as Editor in Chief of The New York Daily News . What I’m doing is talking to them about innovation and disruption in the news industry. I think that everything is going well, but my students will ultimately be the ones to judge me.
TUMBLR-00081.quote: Kevin Convey brought his experience as Editor in Chief of The New York Daily News into the classroom to teach students about innovation and disruption in the news industry, letting them be the ultimate judges of his success.
TUMBLR-00081.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00079.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20 prof brings us 'Obama Revealed' A quick programming note… Professor Jason Samuels’ latest documentary project is scheduled to air on CNN tonight at 8:00 p.m. EST. The program includes original sit-down interviews with President Obama, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Former White House Chief of Staff Rahm Emanuel, Former Director of White House Economic Council Larry Summers, the former Chairs of the President’s Council of Economic Advisers Austan Goolsbee and Christina Romer, Senior Campaign Strategist David Axelrod, Senior Adviser Valerie Jarrett, House Speaker John Boehner, Senator Olympia Snowe, Obama biographer and Washington Post associate editor David Maraniss, Rice University Professor and Historian Douglas Brinkley, New York Times Chief Washington Correspondent David Sanger, former personal aide Reggie Love and Obama supporter Velma Hart. Watch, Tweet, and let us know what you think: @profsamuels_nyu @studio20NYU 0 notes
TUMBLR-00079.quote: Professor Jason Samuels' documentary 'Obama Revealed,' featuring original interviews with President Obama and senior administration officials, aired on CNN.
TUMBLR-00079.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00073.summary: = Silva Shih has spent her summer working with NYU Stern’s economics professor David Backus on a video project, while also reporting for Taiwanese media. = This summer, Tando Ntunja is interning at Global Grind , a Russell Simmons-owned online entertainment journalism site that focuses on the confluence between hip-hop and pop culture. She has focused on creating compelling health coverage and promoting news content using the right social media tools.
TUMBLR-00073.quote: Studio 20 students spent their summers at the intersection of journalism and emerging media — producing video projects, covering health for hip-hop-focused outlets, and learning to promote news through social tools.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00073.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00713.summary: Rosen criticizes a Salon article that claimed to bust Reddit and citizen journalism hype after the Aurora shootings but failed to produce any actual evidence of the hype it claimed to debunk. He argues the article is itself a form of hype -- a 'linkless hype buster' that pretends to deflate overblown claims that were never actually made.
RECORD-00713.quote: The linkless hype buster is a form of hype. It is getting carried away.
RECORD-00713.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00071.summary: “I mean charting your own path, with or without the help of an established journalistic institution, and, most importantly, not waiting for someone else’s permission to do something innovative.” And while Holmes has found success with some big-name media outlets, that may not be the only way to get your ideas out there. Any schlub like me can create a YouTube account and spit out content I think might be beneficial to viewers. While the success of our videos has largely been driven through more institutional channels, guys like Kevin T. Porter who created the Sorkinisms supercut will tell you that if a video is well-timed and entertaining (and in our case, we’ll add “informative” to the list), all it takes is a community on Twitter or Reddit to discover it in order to attract a huge audience.
TUMBLR-00071.quote: The core lesson from David Holmes's path is to chart your own course in journalism without waiting for an established institution's permission — anyone can create and distribute content they believe is valuable.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00071.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00071.summary: Rosen introduces the distinction between "tame" and "wicked" problems, arguing that many issues facing society, such as climate change and failing public schools, are wicked problems—complex, ill-defined, and resistant to traditional solutions. The article proposes a new journalistic beat focused on wicked problems, suggesting that it should be a network, pattern-based, global, and reliant on diverse perspectives rather than solely on expert opinions. This beat would highlight the process of grappling with these problems, focusing on narratives of getting stuck and getting unstuck, and acknowledging the role of denial in hindering progress.
RECORD-00071.quote: Wicked problems have these features: It is hard to say what the problem is, to define it clearly or to tell where it stops and starts.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00071.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00731.summary: A Wonkblog post by Rosen about how political polarization has undermined the press. The original content is no longer available at this URL.
RECORD-00731.quote: Political polarization has fundamentally undermined the press's ability to function as a credible civic institution.
RECORD-00731.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00633.summary: Jonathan Stray identifies four ways journalists beat the competition: exclusive leaks from confidential sources, enterprise reporting through public records and legwork, expert interviews, and original analysis. He argues that enterprise reporting — digging through obscure records and finding on-the-record sources — is the most valuable form, yet also the most threatened by the economics of modern journalism.
RECORD-00633.quote: We tend to venerate this kind of scoop, but the journalist is often just a transcription service.
RECORD-00633.author: Jonathan Stray

RECORD-00089.summary: This article presents a conversation between Scott Rosenberg and Jay Rosen about "verification in reverse," a process where previously established truths are challenged. The discussion centers on a Huffington Post article concerning a letter from NASA retirees criticizing the agency's climate research. Rosen defines verification in reverse and explains how it poses a significant problem for journalists who must balance reporting controversies with upholding factual accuracy. He highlights the conflict between science journalists who consider climate change a settled issue and political journalists who focus on partisan debates, emphasizing the reluctance of many political journalists to confront climate change denialism. Rosen suggests that journalists should not only investigate what happened but also determine whether denialism is involved and treat this as news itself.
RECORD-00089.quote: The phenomenon of “verification in reverse” poses a special problem for journalists. On the one hand, they are supposed to report what people are saying. They are supposed to bring us the news of controversies, protests, disagreements. “Conflict makes news,” and all that. On the other hand, verification is their business. If they cannot support that, they cannot support themselves or their users. They are socially useless, in fact, if they cannot stand up for verification.
RECORD-00089.author: Scott Rosenberg

RECORD-00765.summary: Rosen joins Christopher Lydon on Open Source Radio to discuss the media malaise in America, the crisis of trust in journalism, and the structural challenges preventing the press from fulfilling its democratic role. The conversation explores who can inform the public when the press itself is under siege.
RECORD-00765.quote: When the press itself is under siege, the structural failures preventing journalism from fulfilling its democratic role raise an urgent question: who will tell the people?
RECORD-00765.author: Christopher Lydon

TUMBLR-00035.summary: We dispense with cliches like “Why didn’t the news industry invent Facebook?” and plunge our diversely-talented students into real world projects where they can test their ideas against all the practical constraints that make it hard to do new things in journalism. Studio 20 graduate students are trained to understand the partner’s editorial strategy and business model first. However, we do respect your time and when there is a meeting our people are hyper-prepared.
TUMBLR-00035.quote: Studio 20 plunges diversely-talented students into real world projects where they can test their ideas against all the practical constraints that make it hard to do new things in journalism.
TUMBLR-00035.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00644.summary: Rosen recounts a Facebook mishap involving an event invitation. Intending to invite spouses of friends using the "suggest invitees" feature, they accidentally invited thousands of people, including all their friends and their spouses' friends. This resulted in a flood of notifications and inquiries. Due to the event's public setting, Rosen couldn't uninvite everyone or delete the event initially.  With a friend's help, they changed the privacy settings and deleted the event. Rosen shares lessons learned, including the importance of caution with the "select all" feature, carefully checking privacy settings, acting quickly to address problems, seeking help when needed, and following up with those legitimately invited.  Rosen encourages others to share their social media failures.
RECORD-00644.quote: The great thing about this whole episode is that it has sparked a fascinating conversation among my friends about the new rules of friendship, privacy and etiquette in the age of Facebook.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00644.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00034.summary: I’ve been responsible for real-time reporting, engagement, and crowdsourcing efforts at the Daily News since late 2009, though as time went on it became a newsroom-wide effort. I start my new job as social media editor at Fast Company the end of April. Fast Company is a great environment for someone who wants room to experiment and expand their repertoire—a very cool place.
TUMBLR-00034.quote: Fast Company is a great environment for someone who wants room to experiment and expand their repertoire.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00034.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00075.summary: Jay Rosen and Ethan Zuckerman discuss the transformation of journalism in the digital age. Rosen argues that the internet has democratized the freedom of the press, but also fragmented the mass audience. Zuckerman raises concerns about citizen journalism and the potential for misinformation, citing the Mike Daisey scandal. They explore the evolving roles of journalists, the importance of transparency, and the challenges of echo chambers. Rosen emphasizes that journalism is about relaying facts, distinguishing it from political rhetoric. Both discuss the need to support journalists in a changing media landscape and encourage greater public participation and civic dialogue.
RECORD-00075.quote: people realize that they own the freedom of the press.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00075.author: Katie Edgerton (summary), Jay Rosen, Ethan Zuckerman (speakers)

TUMBLR-00032.summary: Watch below: We interviewed Holmes about his newfound success and what it feels like to be working in a relatively new news genre. When the “ Building a Better Explainer ” project came along with ProPublica, I figured, “well people really like the bed bugs song, so I’ll make a song about fracking and see what happens.” We found some great animators, and everything that could go right did. For this last video, Krishanan Vasudevan, and Sharon Shattuck, both graduates of NYU’s News & Doc program, did the animation.
TUMBLR-00032.quote: When the 'Building a Better Explainer' project came along with ProPublica, the instinct was to test whether the song format that worked for bed bugs could work for fracking—and everything that could go right did.
TUMBLR-00032.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00031.summary: The conversation it sparked over diversity—or lack thereof—in Silicon is still being hashed out. “To my surprise our Black In America documentary panel was standing room only. The documentary continues to resonate far beyond my expectations in terms of impact and awareness.
TUMBLR-00031.quote: The Black in America documentary panel was standing room only at SXSW, and the conversation it sparked over diversity—or lack thereof—in Silicon Valley continued to resonate far beyond initial expectations in terms of impact and awareness.
TUMBLR-00031.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00586.summary: The article discusses NPR's new guidelines aimed at addressing "false equivalence" in journalism, where equal weight is given to opposing sides of a story, even if one side is factually inaccurate.  The author praises NPR's commitment to prioritizing truth and fairness to the truth over the appearance of balance, but also includes a reader's example illustrating the ongoing challenges of avoiding false equivalence, particularly in contentious issues.
RECORD-00586.quote: If our sources try to mislead us or put a false spin on the information they give us, we tell our audience. If the balance of evidence in a matter of controversy weighs heavily on one side, we acknowledge it in our reports. We strive to give our audience confidence that all sides have been considered and represented fairly.
RECORD-00586.author: James Fallows

RECORD-00062.summary: Rosen discusses the Citizens Agenda project undertaken by The Guardian and NYU's Studio 20 program to analyze the questions asked at the Republican presidential debates. The study found that the debates focused heavily on certain topics while neglecting others, highlighting a divergence between the press agenda and the concerns of citizens. Rosen advocates for a greater focus on issues like healthcare, Super PACs, and science and technology in future debates.
RECORD-00062.quote: Right. It's a good example of where the press agenda and the citizens agenda diverge.
RECORD-00062.author: Jay Rosen and Studio 20 NYU

TUMBLR-00030.summary: We  also found only two questions about climate   change, four mentioning the  Arab Spring, and one on women’s rights   beyond abortion. And we  wondered: were people eager to hear more about   these scantly covered  issues? What is your opinion on food labeling?” — Sewassbe,   via comments Thanks to a stellar interactive feature from the Guardian team, readers could also vote up what topics they    wanted to hear more about on site.
TUMBLR-00030.quote: Examining the GOP debates, researchers found only two questions about climate change, four mentioning the Arab Spring, and one on women's rights beyond abortion, then turned the gap into a question: were audiences eager to hear more about these scantly covered issues?
TUMBLR-00030.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00582.summary: This article analyzes NPR's revised ethics handbook, highlighting its shift from a credibility-focused, defensive approach to a more affirmative focus on producing trust and prioritizing the audience.  The key change involves a rejection of 'he said, she said' journalism in favor of prioritizing fairness to the truth, even if it means acknowledging imbalances in evidence. The author praises this evolution, arguing that it empowers those within NPR who strive for improved journalistic practices.
RECORD-00582.quote: The mission of NPR, in partnership with its member stations, is to create a more informed public, one challenged and invigorated by a deeper understanding and appreciation of events, ideas, and culture within the United States and across the globe.
RECORD-00582.author: Chris Mooney

TUMBLR-00029.summary: I think that Studio 20 teaches you how to be independent and quick on your feet. I regularly help brainstorm ideas with Anjali about how we can better engage and inform the Daily News community as a whole.

TUMBLR-00029.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00061.summary: The article critiques the Republican primary debates of 2012, highlighting the disparity between the questions asked by journalists and the issues that voters are actually concerned about. It discusses a study by NYU's Studio 20 analyzing the topics covered in the debates and contrasts them with a "citizens agenda" approach, which prioritizes the concerns of the electorate. Rosen proposes shifting campaign coverage to better reflect the priorities of the public and encourages readers to suggest topics they want the candidates to discuss.
RECORD-00061.quote: We're interested in what we have previously called a "citizens agenda" approach to campaign coverage in 2012.
RECORD-00061.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00028.summary: I lead a team of editors to write, edit, blog, publish, and curate news that interest our audience, Arabic language speakers all over the world. A big part of it is keeping an eye on the website’s numbers—the page views, unique visitors, top stories, etc.—and then seeing how we can use that data to create better, more engaging content. I work on a small team that conducts something called “user research” in order to help make our digital product offerings better.

TUMBLR-00028.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00646.summary: Before the 1980s, the Republican Party was similar to the Democratic Party. The Great Realignment saw Ronald Reagan build a new coalition consisting of socially conservative Christians, the wealthy, and the Southern working class, united by exploiting social tensions. The Republican Party then shifted its focus from economic to social issues, fostering resentment towards groups considered the "liberal elite." After Reagan, the party found a new unifying force in attacking the government, though this created internal tension regarding popular programs. The Republican Party is now in crisis, divided by its inability to shrink the government while still protecting popular programs. The party's future is uncertain, possibly fracturing or fading away without a new way to unite its factions.
RECORD-00646.quote: The party is going to have to decide whether its future lies with the evangelical Christians of the heartland or with the secular, pro-business voters of the suburbs. It cannot be the party of both Rick Santorum and Mitt Romney. It has to choose.
RECORD-00646.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00024.quote: With newly established programs, you can either come out of it with a type of education no one has had before, or you can have an awful experience of a program that's not well thought out.
TUMBLR-00024.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00023.summary: It won’t be a single issue, of course, but a basket of top concerns broadly shared by respondents – six to ten, or perhaps as many as a dozen priorities that originate not with journalists or campaign managers, but with voters. That course, taught by Jay Rosen, will have a technologist and newsroom developer as part of the team, Matt Terenzio . “Together, we will arrive at the picture of how people want journalists to cover the election through a number of traditional and non-traditional methods, including sampling science, internet polling, web forms, social media, old fashioned reporting, discussions and debates, experimental features, plus staff and user-generated content.” The announcement was covered by Nieman Lab, where Megan Garber wrote: Studio 20′s role in the project, Rosen told me, will be in part to act as an interactive team that will help with the inflow and engagement of users; students in the program will also conduct research and analysis and think through — perhaps even invent — features and tools that can foster that engagement in new ways, testing them out on The Guardian’s U.S. site.
TUMBLR-00023.quote: Together, we will arrive at a picture of how people want journalists to cover the election through a number of traditional and non-traditional methods — with priorities originating not with journalists or campaign managers, but with voters.
TUMBLR-00023.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00060.summary: The article discusses an effort by Guardian US and NYU's Studio 20 program to create a "citizens agenda" for the 2012 election coverage. This approach aims to shift the focus from the strategic game of who's going to win to what voters want the candidates to be discussing. It describes a project involving the public and local news organizations to identify key issues and hold candidates accountable to those priorities. The ultimate goal is to make campaign coverage more relevant and useful to the public.
RECORD-00060.quote: democracy is about participating, so let's extend that principle to the campaign news system and see if we can make it work.
RECORD-00060.author: Jay Rosen, Amanda Michel

RECORD-00754.summary: Nieman Lab covers the launch of a citizens agenda project between The Guardian and NYU's Studio 20, led by Rosen and Amanda Michel. The project applies civic journalism principles to the 2012 election, asking voters what issues matter most rather than following the horse race. Digital First Media partners to tailor findings to local coverage.
RECORD-00754.quote: When people complain about what's wrong with the coverage and campaign dialogue, there's an opportunity to find out... well, what should the candidates be discussing as they compete for votes in 2012?
RECORD-00754.author: Megan Garber

RECORD-00649.summary: Journalism is undergoing a significant transformation due to technological advancements, evolving economic models, shifting audience expectations, and open-source culture. These changes present both challenges and opportunities. Serious journalism, upholding principles like transparency, accuracy, and accountability, is crucial, especially in the digital age. This involves curating information, fostering community engagement, and providing tools for civic action. Journalists must collaborate, innovate, and adapt, embracing new technologies and storytelling formats. A strong ethical foundation is essential to navigate the complexities of information in the digital landscape. Journalism students are entering a dynamic field and have the opportunity to shape the future of journalism by embracing new approaches, technologies, and community engagement strategies.
RECORD-00649.quote: Their comparative advantage is no longer in telling us what is happening, because we can learn this from multiple other sources. Rather, their real value-added will be in investigating and explaining why something is happening.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00649.author: Jay Rosen

ProPublica’s most recent investigation, “Redistricting: How Powerful Interests Are Drawing You Out of a Vote” examines the opaque methodology behind the process and how its effects can hurt voters. The Redistricting Song definitely does that, with a backbeat.
TUMBLR-00016.quote: Dave combined clever lyrics, a catchy beat, and animation to bring users into a highly complicated subject—redistricting—and how its effects can hurt voters.
TUMBLR-00016.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00632.summary: Jay Rosen, author of "What Are Journalists For?", discusses investigative journalism's role after the 9/11 attacks in an interview with The World's Marco Werman.

RECORD-00632.author: Marco Werman

RECORD-00609.summary: Political journalism's focus on the "Game Story" hinders understanding of the political world. This story prioritizes politicians' strategies and actions within a competitive game, neglecting policy substance, impact on citizens, and diverse perspectives. Rosen argues this approach, often rooted in objective journalism, results in a detached view that makes politics less accessible and more alienating. The solution proposed is a journalism that interprets political struggles, examines policy impacts, and centers on citizens, ultimately fostering a better understanding of the issues. This shift requires a more engaged journalism that helps citizens understand the world, rather than simply reporting on the political game.
RECORD-00609.quote: If you’re still reporting on the game, you’re still part of the problem. Because the game is not the substance. And the substance is what matters.
RECORD-00609.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00648.summary: Rosen identifies three crucial kinds of context often missing in discussions of intellectual history, using Hayek's work as a case study. The first is the specific problem Hayek was addressing, which was how a society of free individuals could achieve optimal resource allocation despite dispersed knowledge. Second, the relevant intellectual tradition, namely the Austrian school, and Hayek's engagement with Mises and subjectivism, is essential. Lastly, the context of the arguments within Hayek's essay "Economics and Knowledge" itself clarifies his focus on coordinating decentralized knowledge through the market process rather than individual plan optimization. Rosen emphasizes that these contextual elements shape the interpretation of Hayek's ideas, differentiating them from the concerns of others like Robbins.
RECORD-00648.quote: When you’re an expert in a field, you forget what it was like to be a novice. You forget that the things that seem obvious to you are not at all obvious to someone who’s just starting out. And so you fail to explain the context of your requests.
RECORD-00648.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00074.summary: NYU's Studio 20 journalism program, directed by Jay Rosen, represents a departure from traditional journalism education. Instead of focusing on training students for specific roles in a stable media industry, Studio 20 emphasizes innovation and collaboration with major media partners on real-world projects. The program's three studios culminate in individual projects where students work with media organizations on public projects, providing valuable experience and potentially leading to job opportunities. While acknowledging the need for further skill development, particularly in data visualization and programming, the program is lauded for its flexibility and adaptability to the evolving media landscape.
RECORD-00074.quote: Studio 20 acknowledges this reality and seeks to find hope and opportunity in a situation that can seem bleak to those considering — or already in the midst of — a career in journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00074.author: Corbin Hiar

RECORD-00077.summary: NPR's media correspondent David Folkenflik interviews Jay Rosen about his concept of the "view from nowhere," which Rosen argues is the media's attempt to appear unbiased and trustworthy. Rosen believes journalists should reveal their backgrounds and convictions to build trust with the public. This contrasts with the traditional view of impartiality, as advocated by Leonard Downie, former executive editor of The Washington Post, who believes that journalists should strive for objectivity and avoid partisanship.
RECORD-00077.quote: The view from nowhere - that's the name Rosen gives to what he says is the media's true ideology, a way of falsely advertising that they can be trusted because they don't have any dog in the fight.
RECORD-00077.author: David Folkenflik

RECORD-00747.summary: NPR's David Folkenflik profiles Rosen's critique of mainstream journalism's ideology of non-ideology, which Rosen calls 'the view from nowhere.' The piece features Rosen arguing for transparency about reporters' perspectives and former Washington Post editor Leonard Downie defending impartiality.
RECORD-00747.quote: I'd like to know something about their background -- like where they're from. If they've been covering a beat for a while, I'd like to know what fascinates them about their beat, what they think are the biggest challenges facing the nation.
RECORD-00747.author: David Folkenflik

RECORD-00768.summary: On the Media discusses Rosen's argument that journalists' claims to have no opinions or ideology are both false and counterproductive. The segment explores his case that transparency about reporters' perspectives would actually build more trust than the pretense of objectivity.
RECORD-00768.quote: Journalists' claims to have no opinions or ideology are both false and counterproductive — transparency about reporters' perspectives would build more trust than the pretense of objectivity.
RECORD-00768.author: Brooke Gladstone

RECORD-00769.summary: On the Media covers Rosen's campaign to get Sunday talk shows to incorporate fact-checking. The segment discusses his argument that shows like Meet the Press fail viewers by letting guests make false claims unchallenged, and reports on ABC's adoption of PolitiFact verification on This Week.
RECORD-00769.quote: Shows like Meet the Press fail viewers by letting guests make false claims unchallenged, and incorporating fact-checking, as ABC did with PolitiFact on This Week, is a correctable problem.
RECORD-00769.author: Brooke Gladstone

RECORD-00599.summary: And if today the White House press corps can’t get an explanation for Goss’s departure, it will fail some basic test of usefulness. What will the new press secretary do when asked to provide an explanation that was glaringly missing on Friday? But when reason-giving disappears from the governing style of an Administration, it’s not clear what we’re supposed to do.
RECORD-00599.quote: Technology will reshape news gathering and distribution.
RECORD-00599.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00899.summary: Episode 76, mid-December 2010. The conversation continues the show's Wikileaks coverage — by this point the State Department cables release was several weeks old and the press response was the through-line. Jay and Dave also riff on listener mail comparing their voices to Jeff Bridges and Wallace Shawn.
RECORD-00899.quote: Wikileaks continued, plus the recurring listener joke about Dave-as-Jeff-Bridges and Jay-as-Wallace-Shawn.
RECORD-00899.author: Jay Rosen; Dave Winer

TUMBLR-00036.summary: Shirky, who recently published Cognitive Surplus: Creativity and Generosity in a Connected Age (Penguin Press HC, 2010), is currently an associate teacher at the Interactive Telecommunications Program (ITP) in the Kanbar Institute of Film and Television at the Tisch School. By bridging the two departments, Shirky will be able to create on NYU’s campus a range of perspectives on the conversation about the Internet’s capacity to convene groups of people and effectively gather and disseminate information.” “It’s a thrill to be able to return Clay Shirky’s embrace of journalism, as the field’s courtship with technology grows ever deeper,” said Brooke Kroeger, director of the Carter Journalism Institute. Earlier this year, Fortune named Shirky to its “Smartest People in Tech” list, which also included Mark Zuckerberg, Steve Jobs, and Jeff Bezos.
TUMBLR-00036.quote: By bridging the two departments, Shirky will be able to create on NYU's campus a range of perspectives on the conversation about the Internet's capacity to convene groups of people and effectively gather and disseminate information.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00036.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00647.summary: A recurring pattern in responses to criticism involves claiming the critic "just doesn't get it," often employed to avoid directly addressing the substance of the critique. This tactic is frequently used by politicians, pundits, and online commentators. Rosen identifies two potential causes: a simple misunderstanding stemming from differing ideas of clarity, or deliberate vagueness in the initial statement. The latter allows speakers to maintain flexibility, deflecting criticism by claiming misinterpretation or difficulty on the critic's part, enabling them to present ideas without the risk of being clearly contradicted. Rosen observes this trend particularly in online discussions about social media, blogging, and politics, prompting an examination of its frequent use.
RECORD-00647.quote: This way of responding to critics seems to immunize Christianity against any rational criticism. For any objection, no matter how powerful, one can always draw a distinction that the critic has failed to draw.
RECORD-00647.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00637.summary: Rosen dissects Julian Assange's refusal to address rape allegations during a Guardian reader Q&A session in December 2010. Assange claimed the Guardian asked him not to answer, but Rosen argues this was a false impression — it was his lawyer, not the newspaper, keeping him quiet. Rosen warns that Assange's evasiveness was eroding support among the very people who had defended him and funded WikiLeaks.
RECORD-00637.quote: But in the real world, when a man is accused of rape by two different women and he refuses to answer any questions about it, we have a different word for that. And the word is not “smear campaign.” The word is “guilty as hell.”
RECORD-00637.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00033.summary: In the spring of 2011, we’ll devote a whole graduate course (18  students, two instructors, plus consultants) to producing explainers  that we hope ProPublica can publish, as well as a kind of tool kit to  make the task easier. Another group is building Explainer.net ’s  WordPress website, which sometimes means teaching themselves and each  other skills on an ad hoc basis. But they’ll also be reaching far outside the media world to research  techniques used in many different fields.
TUMBLR-00033.quote: In spring 2011, an entire graduate course of 18 students and two instructors was devoted to producing explainers for ProPublica, reaching far outside the media world to research explanation techniques used across many different fields.
TUMBLR-00033.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00753.summary: Nieman Lab reports on a collaboration between ProPublica and Rosen's Studio 20 class at NYU to create better explainer journalism. Students launched Explainer.net to catalog the best explainer techniques and partnered with ProPublica to build new formats for conveying complex information about issues like the foreclosure crisis and healthcare.
RECORD-00753.quote: Journalists love starting from zero and gaining mastery. What they disgorge by way of story is quite inadequate to what they learned. Creating containers, formats, genres, tricks, tools to make that knowledge available is part of the project.
RECORD-00753.author: Lois Beckett

RECORD-00638.summary: Rosen discusses the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), acknowledging its existence for security but criticizing its ineffectiveness and infringement on civil liberties. After widespread complaints, major news outlets and even the White House are now addressing the issue, offering a glimmer of hope for positive change.
RECORD-00638.quote: What Howard Kurtz is doing is playing the classic apologist’s role. He’s taking the government’s side in what is a very real controversy, and he’s doing it by taking down the very reporters who finally got the story right.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00638.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00027.summary: Anjali Khosla Mullany is establishing a noise beat for the New York Times Local East Village . She has also been developing new ideas for the company’s Twitter site and making recommendations. Matylda Czarnecka is working with PBS’ Channel Thirteen to prototype a website and show about the New York City startup ecosystem.
TUMBLR-00027.quote: Studio 20 students embedded with media partners to prototype new digital products, from a noise beat for the New York Times to a website about New York City's startup ecosystem for PBS.
TUMBLR-00027.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00643.summary: Rosen recounts a conversation about Thomas Frank's criticism of consumer culture, specifically citing an article on the film Fight Club as an example. Initially believing Frank wrote the piece, Rosen later learned it was actually written by Andrew Potter. Rosen, a long-time admirer of Frank, was surprised and corrected their friend. Rosen's post acknowledges the mistake, credits Andrew Potter for the piece, and provides a link to it.
RECORD-00643.quote: There is a good deal more to this story than Frank chooses to tell.
RECORD-00643.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00076.summary: This Q&A explores the concept of the "View from Nowhere" in journalism, a term borrowed from philosopher Thomas Nagel. Rosen critiques its unearned authority in American newsrooms, arguing it encourages bad habits and hinders trust. He advocates for a pluralistic approach, where journalists with transparent perspectives coexist with those adhering to impartiality.
RECORD-00076.quote: In fact, American journalism is dumber than most journalists, who often share my sense of absurdity about these practices.
RECORD-00076.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00026.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20's Niel Bekker Publishes Post about Disruptive Storytelling Studio 20’s Niel Bekker recently published a post exploring two new startups, Storify and Qwiki , which are finding ways to disrupt storytelling. From Rosen's post: Which is more disruptive: connecting users to a library of machine-made  knowledge remixes, or connecting users to each other’s curated content,  shaped into narrative by human hands? #Studio 20 #Niel Bekker #Storify #Qwiki #MemeBurn #published work #technology #journalism memeburn.com 0 notes
TUMBLR-00026.quote: Which is more disruptive: connecting users to a library of machine-made knowledge remixes, or connecting users to each other's curated content, shaped into narrative by human hands?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00026.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00025.quote: Studio 20 students collaborated with the New York Daily News to liveblog the NYC Marathon, filling a coverage gap when the paper's running blogger was participating in the race herself.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00025.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00787.summary: Rosen argues for how public media should respond to political efforts to cut its funding, making the case that public broadcasting needs to articulate a stronger public interest justification for its existence beyond just producing good programming.
RECORD-00787.quote: Public media facing defunding efforts needs to articulate a stronger public interest justification for its existence — producing good programming is not, by itself, a sufficient argument for public support.
RECORD-00787.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00018.summary: I am now about half way through the rewriting stage. I published articles on bullet trains , sugar cane and Brazilian cowboys that were picked up by the Washington Post, New York Times  International,  Scientific American and the Guardian, among others (Due  to licensing agreements with Reuters the content is no longer available  on these sites). Over the summer, I was also awarded a grant from the Hugh Fulton Byas Memorial Fund towards my third and final semester with Studio 20.
TUMBLR-00018.quote: James Matthews published articles on bullet trains, sugar cane, and Brazilian cowboys that were picked up by the Washington Post, New York Times International, Scientific American, and the Guardian.
TUMBLR-00018.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00898.summary: Episode 67 features a guest conversation with Saul Hansell, then programming director of AOL's Seed.com content marketplace and previously a long-time New York Times technology reporter. The discussion covers algorithmic content commissioning and the shift from staff bylines to networked freelance contribution.
RECORD-00898.quote: Guest: Saul Hansell, programming director of AOL's Seed.com and former New York Times technology reporter.
RECORD-00898.author: Jay Rosen; Dave Winer

TUMBLR-00014.summary: Each year Studio 20 recruits a mix of writers, editors, videographers, audio journalists, programmers, designers, Web producers and smart people who may have no journalism training at all— under the principle of “bring skills, share skills, learn new stuff.” Recruiting emphasizes students comfortable in more than one medium and ready to tackle new challenges. In the spring of 2013 that site evolved into Bedford + Bowery , which is co-published by NYU Journalism and New York Magazine (nymag.com). (The initial deadline is Jan. 3, 2014; we will accept applications after that but cannot guarantee space or financial aid.
TUMBLR-00014.quote: Studio 20 recruits writers, editors, videographers, programmers, and designers under the principle of 'bring skills, share skills, learn new stuff,' emphasizing students comfortable across multiple media.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00014.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00017.summary: ¶ ● Congratulations to Studio 20’s Tim Stenovec for getting his Local East Village video on a makeshift Hare Krishna center picked up by the Huffington Post! #Studio 20 #Local East Village #Tim Stenovec #video #Huffington Post #East Village 1 note

RECORD-00774.summary: Dan Kennedy at Media Nation writes about Rosen's personal essay on PressThink titled 'Why I Am Not a Journalist: A True Story.' Kennedy notes they both edited college newspapers in the late 1970s and describes Rosen's story of not getting hired at the Buffalo Courier-Express as 'both amusing and a little sad, conjuring up a newspaper world that no longer exists.'
RECORD-00774.quote: Rosen's story of not getting hired at the Buffalo Courier-Express conjures up a newspaper world that no longer exists, making it both amusing and a little sad.
RECORD-00774.author: Dan Kennedy

TUMBLR-00013.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20 Summer: Focus on Lesley Messer This is the first post in a series on how Studio 20 students spent their summers. Lesley Messer tells us about writing for People Magazine and a trip to Toronto: Over the summer, I went back to my full-time job, writing, reporting and fact-checking entertainment features for People . A few highlights included spending time with the cast of Jersey Shore and their families (including Snooki), [read Lesley’s article here ], celebrating the life and career of Golden Girl Rue McClanahan and recently, reporting and co-authoring our cover story on the MTV show Teen Mom.
TUMBLR-00013.quote: Lesley Messer spent her summer writing, reporting, and fact-checking entertainment features for People Magazine — illustrating how Studio 20 students move fluidly between academic training and professional newsroom work.
TUMBLR-00013.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00764.summary: Joe Romm at ThinkProgress reprints Rosen's extended comment explaining why climate science reporting fails. Rosen argues that journalism's commitment to neutrality breaks down when confronting manufactured controversies like climate denial, because the press has no instructions for how to react when 'report both sides' reaches its natural limits. He identifies the problem as structural: the same ideology that protects journalism from government also prevents it from calling out illegitimate debate.
RECORD-00764.quote: Neutrality and objectivity carry no instructions for how to react when they reach their natural limits. And so journalists tend to deny that there are such limits. But with this denial they've violated the code of the truth-teller because these limits are real. See the problem?
RECORD-00764.author: Joe Romm

RECORD-00650.summary: Many high school students lack even a basic understanding of fundamental concepts such as the Constitution, Bill of Rights, and scientific theories, according to the National Assessment of Educational Progress results. A significant percentage of students score below basic in U.S. History, Civics, and Science, indicating a failure to grasp essential knowledge. Rosen believes this lack of education harms both students and the country, hindering informed participation in democracy and the ability to critically evaluate information. Addressing this issue requires a renewed focus on educating youth to ensure a healthy and functional democracy.
RECORD-00650.quote: We are armed not with knowledge of things, but acquaintance with them.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Not the odds but the stakes
RECORD-00650.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00012.summary: MediaShift profiled NYU’s Studio 20 concentration as an example of journalism education adapting to the changing media industry. That’s where Rich  Jones, editor of the LEV, comes in. “We’ll  obviously bring professional level standards to the treatment of those  issues, being under the Times banner brings certain responsibilities,”  said Jones, a former New York Times writer.
TUMBLR-00012.quote: NYU's Studio 20 was profiled as an example of journalism education adapting to the changing media industry, with students working under professional-level standards alongside established news organizations like the New York Times.
TUMBLR-00012.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00009.summary: ¶ ● In case you missed it, last night on CNN, Studio 20 Professor Jason Samuels produced Soledad O'Brien’s live one-hour exclusive interview with Imam Feisal of the controversial Park 51 project. The interview has  been cited in numerous news reports. #Jason Samuels
TUMBLR-00009.quote: Studio 20 Professor Jason Samuels produced Soledad O'Brien's live one-hour exclusive CNN interview with Imam Feisal of the controversial Park 51 project, demonstrating students working at the level of professional broadcast journalism.
TUMBLR-00009.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00008.summary: It took a while before those outside of the government began gaining access to information and developed ways to communicate what went on behind closed doors, and when they did, they began changing the culture of news around diplomacy: Let’s jump ahead to Paris in 1919 and the Peace Conference that ended World War I. At  previous international conferences intended to conclude wars and settle  borders, the diplomats would negotiate in secret and emerge weeks later  with a result which was then conveyed to the home countries as a more  or less finished product. Professional journalism,  which dates from the 1920s, has lived its entire life during this phase,  but let me say it again: this is what your generation has a chance to  break free from.
TUMBLR-00008.quote: At previous international conferences, diplomats negotiated in secret and presented results as finished products; when professional journalism gained access, it began changing the culture of news around diplomacy by communicating what happened behind closed doors.
TUMBLR-00008.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

TUMBLR-00007.summary: From the press release : The site will feature a Virtual Assignment Desk, an interactive digital  platform that has been created as a Wordpress plug-in. These  include pre-college and college tracks as well as a select number of  three-month graduate-level LEV internships , credit and non-credit, available on a competitive basis. #Studio 20 #Jay Rosen #Assignment Desk #Wordpress #Plugin #hyperlocal #journalism #news nyu.edu 0 notes

concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
TUMBLR-00007.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00651.summary: The article explores how the definition of "media" is changing and the impact on those who work in journalism. As new forms of information dissemination emerge, like blogging and citizen journalism, Rosen questions the need for a new term to describe journalists who uphold traditional journalistic principles and work within established media institutions. Rosen proposes calling these individuals "traditional journalists" or "professional journalists" to differentiate them within the evolving media landscape and acknowledge their continued significance.
RECORD-00651.quote: The people formerly known as the audience are those who were on the receiving end of a media system that ran one way, in a broadcasting pattern, with high entry fees and a few firms competing to speak loudly while the rest of the population listened in isolation from one another— and who today are not in a situation like that at all.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00651.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00782.summary: Rosen offers advice to the next generation of journalists, building on his 'people formerly known as the audience' framework. He argues that new journalists must understand the changed relationship between press and public and adapt their practice accordingly.
RECORD-00782.quote: The next generation of journalists must understand that the people formerly known as the audience are now participants, and that changed relationship requires a fundamentally different practice.
RECORD-00782.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00773.summary: Poynter covers Rosen's reflections on why he chose to become a journalism professor and press critic rather than a practicing journalist, despite his early desire to enter the field. The piece explores how his academic path gave him a different vantage point on the profession.
RECORD-00773.quote: Choosing an academic path over the newsroom gave Rosen a different vantage point on the profession — one from which he could study journalism rather than simply practice it.
RECORD-00773.author: Poynter staff

RECORD-00752.summary: Rosen articulates his concept of 'the future of context' -- arguing that news stories need persistent, updatable background documents that help audiences understand ongoing stories. He uses the metaphor of receiving software updates without having the software installed, calling for a 'second part of the news system which gives people a sense of mastery over a big story.'
RECORD-00752.quote: Where does the news accumulate as understanding?
RECORD-00752.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00799.summary: Recap of Rosen's lecture to Australian journalism students about the citizens agenda approach to campaign coverage, arguing that journalists should begin by asking voters what they need to know to cast an informed vote rather than following the horse race.
RECORD-00799.quote: Journalists covering campaigns should start by asking voters what they need to know to cast an informed vote, rather than defaulting to horse-race coverage that serves the profession's interests more than the public's.
RECORD-00799.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00193.summary: Rosen proposes a "Citizen's Agenda" approach to campaign coverage, arguing that journalists should prioritize voters' concerns rather than focusing solely on the "horse race." Rosen outlines a ten-step process for creating and implementing this agenda, involving extensive community engagement, feedback loops, and prioritizing voters' questions in campaign reporting. Rosen contends that this approach improves the quality of political discourse and counters the negative aspects of typical election coverage, even acknowledging potential conflict with candidates who might resist this approach.
RECORD-00193.quote: What does the electorate want the candidates to be discussing as they campaign for votes in this year’s election?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00193.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00783.summary: Rosen presents his 'future of context' concept to ABC Australia staff, arguing for persistent, updatable background documents that provide context to ongoing news stories rather than relying on daily news dispatches alone.
RECORD-00783.quote: Rather than relying on daily dispatches that assume no prior knowledge, journalism should maintain persistent, updatable background documents that give ongoing stories the context they need.
RECORD-00783.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00033.summary: This is an interview with Jay Rosen, a press critic, writer, and professor of Journalism at New York University, discussing horse-race journalism, its impact on the public, and alternative models for reporting election campaigns. Rosen advocates for a 'citizens' agenda' approach, where journalists focus on the issues that matter most to the public. He also discusses the role of the internet and social media in news consumption, and the challenges and opportunities they present for traditional media organizations.
RECORD-00033.quote: horse race journalism is sort of a a reusable model for how to do campaign coverage in which you focus on who's going to win rather than um what the country needs to settle by electing a prime minister
RECORD-00033.author: ABC News (Australia)

RECORD-00780.summary: Rosen is interviewed on Australia's Lateline program about horse race journalism during his visit to Australia, discussing how political coverage fixates on polls, strategy, and who's winning rather than policy substance and public interest.
RECORD-00780.quote: Horse race journalism fixates on polls, strategy, and who's winning rather than policy substance and what the public actually needs to know.
RECORD-00780.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00325.summary: Rosen analyzes the Wikileaks release of the Afghanistan war logs, focusing on Wikileaks' strategy of releasing documents to select major newspapers while simultaneously posting them online. Rosen discusses the implications of Wikileaks' stateless nature and its challenge to traditional notions of journalistic verification and the power dynamic between the state, the press, and a new type of non-state media organization. He also explores the potential for large-scale revelations to generate surprisingly muted public reactions, suggesting a cognitive dissonance in how we expect investigative journalism to impact public discourse and policy.
RECORD-00325.quote: We tend to think: big revelations mean big reactions. But if the story is too big and crashes too many illusions, the exact opposite occurs.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00325.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00137.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20 Student Scores Fellowship to Work for New York Observer; Will Donate Equipment to Program Studio 20 student Amir Shoucri is helping the New York Observer develop their video strategy this summer. I’ll be working there through September, and hopefully will get to produce some interesting content. I’m super psyched to be using an incredible camera with a solid lens and all-digital workflow, and I can’t wait til everyone gets to try it out!
TUMBLR-00137.quote: A Studio 20 student is helping the New York Observer develop their video strategy for the summer, working with an all-digital workflow and professional camera equipment.
TUMBLR-00137.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00897.summary: Episode 58. Jay and Dave work through several items from the past week that hit the show's recurring themes: platform behavior, the press response to it, and the gap between newsroom assumptions and how the open web actually works.
RECORD-00897.quote: Several classic Rebooting The News topics from the prior week, including platform behavior and press response.
RECORD-00897.author: Jay Rosen; Dave Winer

TUMBLR-00136.summary: way to go Cavs!”, “he didn’t care about his fans, even though we had his back thru and thru” and “oh god, whats gonna happen to that huuuge poster of lebron downtown? Yea I said it!” After the decision, however, he didn’t appear to be heartbroken. Chris Bosh, @chrisbosh on Twitter and LeBron’s future fellow teammate, reacted by tweeting “Yeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

RECORD-00580.summary: This article responds to Jay Rosen's advice for journalists, largely agreeing with his emphasis on transparency and accountability but adding considerations about judgment and the limits of self-disclosure. The author argues that while journalists should strive for transparency and avoid opacity as a tool of power, they must also recognize trade-offs and acknowledge the complexities of personal bias.  The author questions the feasibility and value of extensive personal ideological disclosure, suggesting that a journalist's body of work should speak for itself and that excessive self-reflection can detract from journalistic practice.
RECORD-00580.quote: I don't like people who lie, cheat, or steal, or who dissemble for the sake of acquiring or using power, or who think narrowly about everything rather than broadly; who hold fast to dogma; who are quick to condemn those who refuse to condemn.
RECORD-00580.author: Marc Ambinder

RECORD-00376.summary: Rosen argues that journalistic objectivity, as traditionally practiced, is a form of persuasion designed to build trust by appearing unadorned and fact-based.  However, this approach, characterized by phrases like “just the facts,” is inherently flawed because all journalism involves judgment. Rosen proposes shifting away from the "View from Nowhere" toward greater transparency and a plurality of approaches, allowing journalists to express viewpoints while maintaining rigorous reporting standards. This shift is necessary to address declining trust in the press in the era of the internet and audience atomization.
RECORD-00376.quote: Reporting has authority because the reporter did the work.
RECORD-00376.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00135.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20 professor joins CNN as lead producer Congrats to Studio 20’s Professor Jason Samuels who recently left BET to join CNN as a lead producer for CNN’s award-winning, long-form documentary unit ‘In America" - which strives to present untold stories in underreported communities. Professor Samuels’ first prime time documentary for CNN will air in the fall. Learn more about CNN’s “In America” here .
TUMBLR-00135.quote: Studio 20 professor Jason Samuels joined CNN as a lead producer for its long-form documentary unit 'In America,' which focuses on presenting untold stories from underreported communities.
TUMBLR-00135.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00420.summary: Rosen analyzes the Politico's reporting on General McChrystal's resignation, focusing on a paragraph initially published and later redacted, which suggested that beat reporters are less likely to report negatively on powerful figures to maintain access.  Rosen explores whether this observation is accurate and criticizes the Politico's decision to remove the paragraph and refuse to explain the edit, viewing it as a case of self-censorship to protect the reputation of beat reporters.
RECORD-00420.quote: I love a good conspiracy as much as the next guy, but this aint one.
RECORD-00420.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00519.summary: Jay Rosen responds to Marc Ambinder's critique of Rosen's article "Clowns to the Left of Me, Jokers to the Right."  Rosen clarifies his previous argument, emphasizing the distinction between journalism and ideological argument. He argues that while objectivity is not always achievable, journalists should strive for transparency and acknowledge when the truth is hard to ascertain. Rosen proposes a shift away from the 'view from nowhere' towards greater disclosure of journalists' perspectives, allowing readers to understand the context of their reporting.
RECORD-00519.quote: To stand back and look at a situation dispassionately is vital to accuracy, and in a sense to intellect itself. My almost foolproof measure of intellectual honesty is the ability to paraphrase the arguments of another such that the other recognizes his or her view in the paraphrase.
RECORD-00519.author: Jay Rosen

TUMBLR-00134.summary: Set to launch this fall, the site will be produced at NYU and featured on nytimes.com. “You have to have an elegant hinge so that the problems of coordinating two institutions don’t overwhelm you,” Rosen said in a phone interview. #New York Times #The Local #East Village #Jay Rosen #Rich Jones #Poynter 1 note
TUMBLR-00134.quote: "You have to have an elegant hinge so that the problems of coordinating two institutions don't overwhelm you," Rosen said of the NYU-New York Times partnership to produce a local news site for the East Village.
TUMBLR-00134.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20

RECORD-00270.summary: Rosen challenges the common perception that the ideology of the US political press is easily definable as either liberal or conservative. Rosen argues that the press's apparent ideology is far more complex, shaped by factors such as journalists' cosmopolitanism, their pursuit of authoritative narratives that disrupt established viewpoints, and their inherent preference for 'good stories' which often highlight negative events. This results in a complex dynamic where journalists, while often personally liberal, generate narratives that are not consistently aligned with either the left or right. Rosen illustrates this complexity through analysis of journalist behaviors and the contrasting interpretations of their work from both sides of the political spectrum.
RECORD-00270.quote: In the sphere of deviance we find “political actors and views which journalists and the political mainstream of society reject as unworthy of being heard.” As in the sphere of consensus, neutrality isn’t the watchword here; journalists maintain order by either keeping the deviant out of the news entirely or identifying it within the news frame as unacceptable, radical, or just plain impossible…
RECORD-00270.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00779.summary: Rosen presents his 'new media maxims' to World Bank staff, outlining principles for understanding the digital media landscape including audience engagement, the shift from one-to-many to many-to-many communication, and the implications for institutions that rely on public communication.
RECORD-00779.quote: Digital media has shifted communication from one-to-many to many-to-many, and institutions that rely on public communication must reckon with what that shift demands of them.

RECORD-00489.summary: Rosen discusses the impact of the internet and social media on audience engagement, particularly at conferences.  Rosen, Jay Rosen, introduces the concept of "audience atomization overcome," describing how audiences, once isolated, are now connected horizontally (peer-to-peer) and vertically (to speakers/institutions). This interconnectedness significantly increases the risk for unprepared speakers, raising the bar for presentations. The article then provides ten strategies for avoiding negative feedback in this new context, emphasizing pre-event planning, audience engagement, and incorporating audience feedback during presentations.
RECORD-00489.quote: The people formerly known as the audience, once connected up to big institutions and centers of power, but not across to one another, have overcome their own atomization, which was a normal condition during the age of mass media. With the rise of social media and mobile devices they are now connected horizontally, peer to peer, at the same time as they connect vertically: to the news, the program, the speaker, the spectacle.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00489.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00654.summary: Legitimacy in journalism hinges on several key terms. Expertise is demonstrated through experience and knowledge. Independence, crucial for separating news from propaganda, requires journalists to avoid being swayed by external agendas. Objectivity involves presenting stories fairly and accurately. Transparency demands that journalists disclose their sources and methods. Accountability requires taking responsibility for errors and upholding ethical standards. Impartiality means treating all parties equally. Serving the public interest, by providing relevant information and promoting informed debate, is essential. Verification, through cross-referencing and fact-checking, is crucial for maintaining credibility, especially in the era of misinformation. These elements work together to ensure news is trustworthy and serves the public good.
RECORD-00654.quote: The primary obligation of a journalist is to the public.
RECORD-00654.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00659.summary: When considering the wisdom of crowds, it's crucial to avoid blanket statements and recognize the nuanced nature of crowd behavior. It's essential to reject the notion that all crowds or their decisions are inherently wise or always wrong. Factors like emotion, misinformation, and groupthink can sway crowds. Individuals shouldn't automatically assume they are correct when disagreeing with a crowd, nor should they always go against the crowd. There are varying types of crowd wisdom, and the ability to discern when a crowd is wise isn't always obvious. Learning from crowds, even "dumb" ones, is possible, and blindly following or rejecting the crowd should be avoided. The key lies in understanding when and what aspects of crowd behavior should be rejected.
RECORD-00659.quote: When you’re thinking about whether to trust a crowd, the question isn’t whether you believe in the wisdom of crowds or not; the question is, are the conditions right for the crowd to be wise?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00659.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00656.summary: Jay Rosen's checklist offers a framework for ethical journalism, focusing on the impact of actions rather than perfect moral behavior. The checklist, developed for students and newsrooms, comprises eight key components: transparency regarding methods and motives; admitting and correcting mistakes; involving the community in newsgathering; showing empathy and humanity towards subjects; actively listening to audiences and sources; ensuring fairness and proportionality in reporting; practicing humility and self-doubt; and demonstrating courage. These principles aim to guide journalists in adapting their ethical practices amidst changes in the field, encouraging accountability and a rational, transparent approach to reporting.
RECORD-00656.quote: If you were on the receiving end of the story you are reporting and writing, would you feel that you were being treated fairly?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

RECORD-00657.summary: Rosen reflects on a conversation about Obama's call for transparency and expresses skepticism about its feasibility given the political system's reliance on secrecy. RECORD-00657.quote: I suspect the press embraces savviness because it makes them feel like insiders. The rest of us may believe a candidate when he says he will do something, but they know better. They’ve seen it all before.

RECORD-00655.summary: The Republican Party in Texas faces internal challenges, despite its history of electoral success. However, the party's conservative principles, like low taxes and regulations, remain popular, and the state's growing population brings in new conservative voters. The Republican Party can succeed in Texas by addressing the primary issues and re-integrating moderate viewpoints. The future of the party in Texas is promising, but requires effort.
RECORD-00655.quote: What you are witnessing is the de-bugging of the software that runs in the heads of Washington journalists. The software is called, “the view from nowhere.”

RECORD-00585.summary: The author critiques Jay Rosen's optimistic view on the decline of "he said, she said" journalism.  While acknowledging that sophisticated journalists recognize the flaws of false balance, the author argues that economic pressures in the media industry, including job cuts and the loss of specialized journalists, make the lazy shortcut of "he said, she said" reporting even more prevalent. The author concludes that the blogosphere's ability to counteract this trend is limited due to the underlying economic realities of the media business.
RECORD-00585.quote: There's a reason the critique of false "balance" emerged, in significant part, from the science journalism world. In CJR, I was very much channeling the complaints of many evolutionary and climate scientists, who were outraged by media coverage and continually pointed out that since there's no such thing as "balance" in science, reporting about science which employs such a paradigm often gets the story completely wrong.
RECORD-00585.author: Chris Mooney

RECORD-00387.summary: Rosen critiques the "he said, she said" style of journalism, arguing that it often fails to assess competing truth claims and instead offers a false sense of balance.  Rosen contends that this approach, while seemingly a quick and easy solution to reporting deadlines and the complexity of verifying information, ultimately hinders truth-telling.  The rise of the internet and readily available information sources have made this style of reporting increasingly untenable, as readily available evidence allows for a more nuanced and accurate presentation of facts, moving beyond a simple recitation of opposing viewpoints.
RECORD-00387.quote: “How much more evidence do you need?” is the kind of exasperation a lot of us have felt with what he calls “false balance,” which is another name for the pattern I’m describing.
RECORD-00387.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00700.summary: Rosen critiques "he said, she said" journalism — the practice of presenting two opposing claims without assessing their truth — arguing that this form of false balance fails the public and should be abandoned.
RECORD-00700.quote: Presenting two opposing claims without assessing their truth is a form of false balance that fails the public and should be abandoned.
RECORD-00700.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00241.summary: The Huffington Post launches the Huffington Post Investigative Fund, a non-profit initiative funded by The Huffington Post and The Atlantic Philanthropies, aimed at producing investigative journalism. Jay Rosen, a senior advisor to the project, discusses its goals, including the use of open-source and distributed reporting methods, collaboration between professional and amateur journalists, and the importance of high verification standards. The Fund aims to 'report once, run anywhere,' making its content freely available for republication. The initiative sparks discussions about the future of investigative journalism, particularly its role in smaller communities.
RECORD-00241.quote: The announcement of its birth, along with the $1.75 million starter budget, is really the launch of a new Internet-based news organization with a focus on original reporting.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00241.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00542.summary: Rosen curates a collection of essays and blog posts from March 2009, forming a 'flying seminar' on the future of news in the face of the newspaper industry's crisis.  The pieces explore various perspectives, from the sociological implications of the decline of the traditional press (Paul Starr, Yochai Benkler) to the internal struggles of news organizations (Clay Shirky) and the potential of new media ecosystems (Steven Berlin Johnson).  The authors discuss the changing production models of news, the potential for citizen journalism, and the challenges of adapting to a rapidly evolving media landscape.
RECORD-00542.quote: Society doesnt need newspapers. What we need is journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00542.author: Jay Rosen

CLIP-00021.summary: This article discusses the website Spot.Us and its efforts to provide funding for freelance journalists, mentioning Jay Rosen as a figure involved in citizen journalism and related projects.
CLIP-00021.quote: Spot.Us pioneered a community-funding model for freelance journalism, reflecting Jay Rosen's broader argument that new institutional forms — not just new technologies — are needed to sustain independent reporting.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
CLIP-00021.author: San Francisco Chronicle

RECORD-00438.summary: This post reflects on Jay Rosen's appearance on Bill Moyers Journal, discussing his article "Audience Atomization Overcome" and the lack of coverage in the mainstream press.
