Rosen highlights the discrepancy between the blogosphere's reception and the silence from the established political press, emphasizing his unique perspective gained from years of studying the national press. He expresses gratitude to Bill Moyers, PBS, and Glenn Greenwald for their support.
RECORD-00438.quote: I have been studying the national press since I received my PhD in 1986. This is the first time I have been able to unfold my own view of it on national television.
RECORD-00438.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00728.summary: Rosen and Glenn Greenwald argue on Bill Moyers Journal that the political press has become an establishment institution with a vested interest in preserving Washington's status quo. Rosen explains that the press cannot consider the possibility that Washington's institutions have failed because the press is one of those institutions. Both guests see the internet as a way to circumvent top-down information exchange and force change.
RECORD-00728.quote: What cannot be considered is that there could be anything radically wrong with Washington. That the entire institution could be broken. That idea doesn't really occur to the press, because they're one of those institutions.
RECORD-00728.author: Bill Moyers; Jay Rosen; Glenn Greenwald

RECORD-00496.summary: Rosen reflects on the relationship between the presidency and the press, tracing its evolution from Theodore Roosevelt's proactive engagement with the media to George W. Bush's strategic distancing.  Rosen argues that Barack Obama's presidency presents an opportunity to redefine this relationship, advocating for greater transparency and a more direct engagement with the public, moving beyond the traditional model of a single interlocutor (the White House press corps) and the dominance of 'Big Media'.  Rosen emphasizes the need for Obama to actively shape the narrative, urging him to 'write it himself' – to control the information flow and actively engage with a broader, more diverse media landscape.
RECORD-00496.quote: What we should care about is not how many questions the press gets to ask at White House news conferences—a hapless metric—but how open to questions the Obama White House is in all the available ways: old, new and recovered.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00496.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00340.summary: Rosen analyzes Daniel C. Hallin's model of the three spheres of journalism (consensus, legitimate debate, and deviance) to explain how the US political press operates. Hallin's model reveals how journalists implicitly define what constitutes acceptable political discourse, often marginalizing dissenting views and reinforcing existing power structures. The rise of the internet and blogging, however, allows like-minded individuals to connect, challenging the press's ability to control the narrative and define consensus, a phenomenon Rosen summarizes as “audience atomization overcome.”
RECORD-00340.quote: The ability to infect us with notions of what’s realistic is one of the most potent powers press and political elites have.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00340.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00699.summary: Rosen introduces the concept of "audience atomization overcome," arguing that the internet allows dispersed individuals to find each other and organize, breaking the monopoly that mass media once held over public attention and narrative.
RECORD-00699.quote: The internet breaks the monopoly that mass media once held over public attention by allowing dispersed individuals to find each other and organize — what Rosen calls 'audience atomization overcome.'
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00699.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00437.summary: Rosen documents Rosen's process of writing a piece about his use of Twitter for the Chronicle of Higher Education.  It details his approach to explaining Twitter to a non-Twitter using audience, outlining the key aspects he plans to cover, and soliciting input from his readers on how they utilize the platform. Rosen frames his Twitter usage as a hand-built tipster network and seeks similar experiences from others to enrich his article.
RECORD-00437.quote: What I have so far: A dummy title. Why I Write 400 Words a Day and Put Them on Twitter. Whether that’s the actual title or not, it’s the question my piece must answer.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00437.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00333.summary: Rosen discusses a shift in the Knight Fellowships at Stanford University, moving away from a model of general enrichment for mid-career journalists to one focused on journalistic innovation and entrepreneurship. The change is driven by the instability of the news industry, with newsrooms increasingly unable to absorb returning fellows or value their newly acquired knowledge. The new model emphasizes the creation of tangible, public goods by fellows, mirroring an open-source approach and aiming to increase the fellowship's impact on journalism beyond the individual level.
RECORD-00333.quote: The people who steer the Knight Stanford program decided it had to become more valuable to the social practice of journalism, worldwide. They don’t necessarily know how to do this, but they want to increase the supply of public goods the fellows create as a result of their year at Stanford.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00333.author: Jay Rosen

CLIP-00020.summary: Article discusses challenges of citizen journalism including the potential for false reporting and verification issues. Mentions that Professor Jay Rosen did not return calls for comment.
CLIP-00020.quote: Citizen journalism carries the real risk of false or unverified reporting, exposing the gap between professional editorial standards and the unfiltered, informal accountability structures of amateur news production.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
CLIP-00020.author: San Francisco Chronicle

RECORD-00329.summary: Rosen explores the evolving relationship between bloggers and journalists in the early days of the internet. Rosen argues that the distinctions between traditional journalism and blogging are less about inherent ethics and more about the different structures of closed and open editorial systems. He highlights the differences in production methods, gatekeeping versus filtering, and the nature of trust in each system. Ultimately, he contends that the success of blogging demonstrates that it has developed its own ethics based on the trust built between bloggers and their audiences within the open platform.
RECORD-00329.quote: If “ethics” are the codification in rules of the practices that lead to trust on the platform where the users actually are—which is how I think of them—then journalists have their ethics and bloggers have theirs.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00329.author: Jay Rosen

CLIP-00053.summary: An article discussing the political controversy over Barack Obama's use of the phrase 'lipstick on a pig' in reference to John McCain's policies. Jay Rosen is quoted saying it doesn't matter whether the outrage is real or contrived.
CLIP-00053.quote: New York University professor Jay Rosen says it doesn't really matter whether the outrage is real or contrived.
CLIP-00053.author: The Post Standard

RECORD-00881.summary: A brief HuffPost morning podcast appearance by Rosen, published in the late stages of the 2008 presidential campaign. HuffPost's modern templated page preserves only the title and publication metadata; full episode audio is not surfaced on the current page.
RECORD-00881.quote: Short HuffPost morning podcast featuring Jay Rosen on press think and the 2008 campaign.
RECORD-00881.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00698.summary: Analysis of former White House press secretary Scott McClellan's memoir and what his account of the Bush administration's media strategy reveals about how the press briefing room was used to obscure rather than illuminate.
RECORD-00698.quote: McClellan's memoir shows how the White House press briefing room — nominally a site of transparency — was systematically used to obscure rather than illuminate the Bush administration's decision-making.
RECORD-00698.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00520.summary: John McCain's selection of Sarah Palin as his running mate is analyzed as a culture war strategy aimed at creating conflict with journalists and bloggers, exploiting the resentment narrative, and focusing on personalities rather than issues.  The strategy hinges on Palin's charisma and the ensuing controversy, leveraging both the intense support from social conservatives and the negative press coverage to generate a wave of attention and fundraising. Rosen notes the risks involved and the uncertainty of the strategy's success.
RECORD-00520.quote: At the center of the strategy is the flashpoint candidacy of Sarah Palin, a charismatic figure around whom the war can be fought to scale, as it were.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00520.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00697.summary: Rosen examines New York Times executive editor Bill Keller's defense of a contested story, analyzing what "I'm proud to stand by this story" reveals about how editors handle criticism and accountability at major newspapers.
RECORD-00697.quote: When Bill Keller said 'I'm proud to stand by this story,' it revealed how editors at major newspapers use professional pride as a shield against accountability rather than as an engagement with legitimate criticism.
RECORD-00697.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00288.summary: Rosen critiques a Mother Jones feature questioning whether Barack Obama's campaign rhetoric exaggerated its historical significance. Rosen challenges the feature's premise, arguing that there's no direct quote or evidence supporting the claim that Obama compared his campaign to past progressive movements. Rosen details their correspondence with Mother Jones editors, revealing a missing contextual speech excerpt that partially justifies the feature's framing, but still leaves crucial aspects unaddressed. The article highlights the dangers of inadvertently creating hype while attempting to debunk it and questions the journalistic rigor of the Mother Jones piece.
RECORD-00288.quote: There’s a moment in the life of every generation, when that spirit has to come through if we are to make our mark on history. And this is our moment. This is our time.
RECORD-00288.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00462.summary: Rosen analyzes the success of "The Giant Pool of Money," a This American Life episode explaining the mortgage crisis.  Rosen argues that the episode's effectiveness stems from its prioritizing of explanation over simply reporting facts. He contends that traditional journalism often fails to provide the necessary background context for understanding complex news events, leading to audience disengagement.  He proposes a shift in journalistic priorities, advocating for the creation of more explanatory pieces that serve as prerequisites for understanding subsequent news reports, thereby increasing audience engagement and comprehension.
RECORD-00462.quote: If explanation is required for information acquisition, then the explainer comes before the informer as a pre-requisite.
RECORD-00462.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00436.summary: Rosen analyzes Brian Ross's response to questions regarding ABC News's inaccurate anthrax reporting in 2001.  Rosen presents a fictional Q&A summarizing Ross's responses, highlighting inconsistencies and raising concerns about the network's handling of the situation, lack of corrections, and potential implications for the relationship between media, government, and the public. The piece also discusses the broader implications of the incident for journalism and its relationship with power in Rosen's post-Iraq War era.
RECORD-00436.quote: The watchdog press died under Bush. We may have a watchdog press again some day, it could be reborn. But it died. And really the only way we’re going to know that full story is through some kind of, almost like a media truth and reconciliation commission, which I have no hope for.
RECORD-00436.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00416.summary: Rosen details a coordinated effort by bloggers and journalists to hold ABC News accountable for its 2001 anthrax reporting, which falsely linked Iraqi involvement.  Rosen, Jay Rosen, and Dan Gillmor posed three key questions to ABC News regarding the sourcing and accuracy of their reporting, emphasizing the importance of transparency and accountability when confidential sources mislead. The response from ABC News, along with commentary from various journalists and publications, highlighted the ethical dilemmas surrounding confidential sources and the need for investigative journalism to correct the record in cases of significant misinformation.
RECORD-00416.quote: A substantially false story that helps make the case for war by raising fears about enemies abroad attacking the United States is released into public debate because of faulty reporting by ABC News.
RECORD-00416.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00257.summary: Rosen explores the definition of citizen journalism, focusing on Rosen's concise definition: "When the people formerly known as the audience employ the press tools they have in their possession to inform one another, that’s citizen journalism." Rosen discusses various perspectives on the term, including those from bloggers and other media analysts, and highlights the implications for the traditional news media, suggesting that citizen journalism represents a shift in how information is created and disseminated, moving away from a model of the press as a singular information pipeline.
RECORD-00257.quote: When the people formerly known as the audience employ the press tools they have in their possession to inform one another, that’s citizen journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00257.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00555.summary: Rosen contrasts two responses to the decline of traditional newspapers.  One is the curmudgeonly resistance of veteran journalists clinging to the past, exemplified by the hostile reactions to a young intern's positive assessment of her editor's restructuring plans. The other is a proactive approach, represented by the Tree House Media Project, which empowers journalists to become self-publishers and adapt to the changing media landscape.  Rosen argues that the future lies in embracing self-reliance and abandoning the 'mass' identity of traditional media in favor of more human-scale approaches.
RECORD-00555.quote: No longer does one need a printing press to publish, only a personal computer, an Internet connection and an idea.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00555.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00180.summary: This 2008 essay by Jay Rosen uses the metaphor of migration to describe the transformation of journalism in the digital age. Rosen argues that professional journalists, facing the decline of their traditional business model, must adapt to a new media landscape characterized by two-way communication, horizontal sharing, and the rise of citizen journalism. He highlights the challenges of this transition, including resistance from within the profession and the need to integrate professional and amateur journalism practices. Rosen uses the example of OffTheBus, a project he co-founded with Arianna Huffington, as an illustration of a distributed reporting model for campaign coverage.
RECORD-00180.quote: The land that newsroom people have been living on—also called their business model—no longer supports their best work.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00180.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00446.summary: This post updates the progress of Beatblogging.org, a project exploring whether beat reporters can improve their work by using social networks.  David Cohn, the original editor, has secured funding for a new project, spot.us, and Patrick Thornton has taken over Beatblogging.org.  The project will continue to profile beat reporters using networked approaches and collaborate with WiredJournalists.com to reach a wider audience of innovative journalists.
RECORD-00446.quote: Maybe a beat reporter could do a way better job if there was a ‘live’ social network connected to the beat, made up of people who know the territory the beat covers, and want the reporting on that beat to be better.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00446.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00361.summary: Rosen details a collaborative project, the "McCain News Hunt," which utilized NewsTrust, a platform for rating and sharing news stories, and OffTheBus to crowdsource the best journalism about John McCain during a specific week. Participants rated 233 stories, resulting in a ranked list highlighting the top-rated pieces and demonstrating the potential of social media and collaborative filtering to improve news discovery and quality in a proliferating media landscape.
RECORD-00361.quote: The results aren’t spectacular or surprising, and I make no large claims for them. They do show that people really like accountability journalism and that Charlie Savage, now of the New York Times, wrote the most important McCain piece that week.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00361.author: Jay Rosen and Gabriel Beltrone

RECORD-00529.summary: Rosen analyzes a case involving Mayhill Fowler, a citizen journalist contributing to OffTheBus, who obtained an off-the-record comment from Bill Clinton.  The incident sparks a debate about the ethics and implications of citizen journalism, particularly concerning transparency, the changing nature of 'off the record' interactions, and the relationship between professional and citizen journalists. Rosen explores the evolving media landscape and questions traditional journalistic practices in light of the increased accessibility of information and the blurring lines between professional and amateur reporting.
RECORD-00529.quote: Professional reporters are going to have to decide whether they want to view citizen journalists as unfair competition, which is one option, or as extending the news net to places that pro reporters can’t, won’t or don’t go, which is another—and I think a better—way to look at it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00529.author: Jay Rosen

CLIP-00087.summary: A column by Kathleen Parker about former White House press secretary Scott McClellan's tell-all book and the Bush administration's media strategy. Parker references New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen's theory that the Bush administration wanted to 'downgrade the press as a player' within the executive branch.
CLIP-00087.quote: McClellan's memoir confirms what Rosen had theorized — that the Bush White House pursued a systematic effort to 'downgrade the press as a player' within the executive branch.
CLIP-00087.author: Kathleen Parker

CLIP-00086.summary: A Kathleen Parker column analyzing Scott McClellan's memoir about the Bush White House. Parker discusses how McClellan was underestimated and how his book reveals the Bush administration's media strategy. She references New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen's analysis that the Bush administration wanted to 'downgrade the press as a player' in the executive branch.
CLIP-00086.quote: The Bush administration's media strategy was not incompetence but intent: to diminish the press as an institutional check on executive power.
CLIP-00086.author: Kathleen Parker

CLIP-00029.summary: Article discusses Scott McClellan's book and analyzes George W. Bush's administration and media strategy. Jay Rosen is mentioned in the context of his theory on the Bush administration's approach to the press.
CLIP-00029.quote: The Bush administration treated the press not as a channel for informing the public but as an obstacle to be managed, a strategy Jay Rosen theorized as defining the White House's relationship with the media.
CLIP-00029.author: The Birmingham News

CLIP-00085.summary: Syndicated column by Kathleen Parker examining whether former White House Press Secretary Scott McClellan's tell-all memoir about the Bush administration makes him dishonorable. Parker references NYU journalism professor Jay Rosen's 'rollback' theory, in which Rosen argued the Bush administration wanted to 'downgrade the press as a player' in governance and reduce its role in holding the White House accountable.
CLIP-00085.quote: The Bush administration sought to 'downgrade the press as a player' in governance, deliberately reducing its role in holding the White House accountable.
CLIP-00085.author: Kathleen Parker

RECORD-00210.summary: Rosen analyzes Scott McClellan's tenure as White House press secretary, arguing that his role was not to communicate effectively but to actively frustrate and delegitimize the press. McClellan's ineffectiveness, far from being accidental, was a deliberate strategy – part of a broader 'Rollback' policy to diminish the press's influence and enhance executive power. This involved minimizing communication, refusing detailed answers, and promoting an environment of non-engagement to reduce the press's ability to hold the administration accountable.
RECORD-00210.quote: McClellan’s job was to contest or deny the ‘terrain of fact,’ the empirical evidence, as traditionally defined.
RECORD-00210.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00528.summary: Rosen analyzes Scott McClellan's post-White House reflections, connecting his experience as press secretary to a broader shift in White House communication strategies under the Bush administration.  Rosen argues that the Bush administration strategically employed non-communication and opacity, rejecting the traditional role of the press as an interlocutor between the presidency and the public. This departure from the Roosevelt-era model, where the president actively engaged with the press, represented a calculated effort to enhance executive power by controlling information flow and avoiding accountability.  McClellan's regret and public acknowledgment of his role in this strategy highlight the consequences of this approach and its ultimate failure in maintaining public support.
RECORD-00528.quote: The ruining of Scott McClellan was part of something way bigger, and to understand it we have to go back to the beginning of the White House press corps.
RECORD-00528.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00576.summary: Rosen discusses Clay Shirky's concept of "cognitive surplus," the vast amount of free time previously consumed by television, and its potential for productive online activity.  Rosen uses Shirky's ideas to explore the shift from passive media consumption to active participation and creation, exemplified by his daughter's blogging activities. He contrasts the passive nature of traditional media with the interactive possibilities of the web, highlighting the need for new media projects to utilize this untapped potential for social good.
RECORD-00576.quote: Someone working alone, with really cheap tools, has a reasonable hope of carving out enough of the cognitive surplus, enough of the desire to participate, enough of the collective goodwill of the citizens, to create a resource you couldn’t have imagined existing even five years ago.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00576.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00199.summary: Rosen details the transformation of the Capital Times, a Madison, Wisconsin newspaper, from a daily print publication to a primarily online news outlet with two weekly print editions. The shift, driven by economic pressures and the changing media landscape, involves job losses, a move to a digital-first strategy, and a re-evaluation of the paper's role in the community. Rosen analyzes the challenges and potential opportunities presented by this transition, considering the competitive online environment and the paper's legacy as a progressive voice in Madison.
RECORD-00199.quote: The presses have stopped but the press goes on.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00199.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00457.summary: Rosen explores the crisis facing newspapers due to the internet's disruption of their traditional business models.  Rosen discusses the challenges of transitioning from an advertising-subsidized model to sustainable alternatives, questioning whether the public good of quality journalism can be maintained. He examines various approaches, including non-profit models like ProPublica, innovative ventures like The Politico, and the potential for filtering and repackaging online content. The article also touches upon the inherent inefficiencies of advertising and the need for increased public understanding of the true cost of serious journalism.
RECORD-00457.quote: The traditional newspaper formula has been patently unworkable for years, but too many newspaper leaders don’t understand that.
RECORD-00457.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00449.summary: Rosen discusses the case of Mayhill Fowler, an Obama supporter and citizen journalist who reported on comments made by Obama at a fundraiser.  Her report, published on the Huffington Post's OffTheBus blog, was picked up by major news outlets but was subsequently downplayed by Meet the Press, leading to a discussion about the evolving role of citizen journalism in political coverage and the challenges faced by traditional media in navigating this new landscape. The article explores the blurred lines between citizen journalist, campaign supporter, and news reporter, highlighting the lack of established frameworks for understanding this emerging phenomenon.
RECORD-00449.quote: The issue is less the distinction between “citizen” and “journalist” and more whether the Founding Fathers ever contemplated such a distinction in the first place.A close reading of the First Amendment and centuries of legal precedent says “no.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00449.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00693.summary: An analysis of the press corps's long-standing favorable relationship with John McCain, examining how the senator cultivated reporters through access and candor, and what this meant for coverage of his 2008 presidential campaign.
RECORD-00693.quote: John McCain cultivated the press through extraordinary access and candor, and reporters rewarded him with favorable coverage — a transactional relationship that shaped how his 2008 presidential campaign was framed long before voters weighed in.
RECORD-00693.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00488.summary: Rosen analyzes the emerging conflict between liberal bloggers and mainstream media regarding their coverage of John McCain's presidential campaign in 2008.  Rosen questions whether a declared 'blogospheric war' against the media is truly underway, or if the situation is more nuanced and dynamic.  The piece examines the media's perceived favoritism towards McCain, the bloggers' strategies to counter this narrative, and the potential impact of McCain's unprecedented openness to press questioning on the campaign.
RECORD-00488.quote: This campaign is not going to be between the Democrats and the Republicans, said Philadelphias Duncan Black, who writes under the name Atrios and whose highly popular progressive political blog, named Eschaton, inspired the gathering of bloggers and political activists called Eschacon ‘08.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00488.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00626.summary: The program features a discussion with media critic and NYU professor Jay Rosen about the current state of news and its role in a divided America. It highlights the business aspects of news in the digital age, while also acknowledging its importance as a public good. The conversation centers on the challenges facing journalism, including shrinking newsrooms, rising disinformation, and declining trust. Rosen advocates for a shift in journalistic approach, urging the press to move beyond objectivity and neutrality to actively defend democracy by calling out misinformation and supporting democratic norms. The discussion also includes the impact of AI on journalism, the future of local news, and the challenge of rebuilding public trust.
RECORD-00626.quote: The idea that there is this large, untapped audience of people in the middle who are just waiting for a news organization to come along and give it to them straight, that’s a fantasy.
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes
RECORD-00626.author: Christopher Lydon

RECORD-00478.summary: Rosen analyzes the unusually positive relationship between John McCain's presidential campaign and the press corps.  Rosen argues that McCain's willingness to engage in extensive, off-the-record conversations with reporters, even when facing tough questions, cultivated a sense of rapport and trust, creating a 'reputational capital' that shielded him from harsher criticism.  Rosen contrasts this with other candidates' more guarded approaches, highlighting how McCain's openness, while potentially containing strategic elements, inadvertently humanized both him and the reporters, resulting in more favorable coverage. The article also explores whether Barack Obama should adopt a similar strategy.
RECORD-00478.quote: The currency in which reporters trade is questions actually answered, QAA. McCain simply realized that the QAA system allowed him to print money, as in: ask all the questions you want!And where does that currency go? Straight into Chuck Todd’s Presumptive Credibility Bank.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00478.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00238.summary: This post critiques CNN's Wolf Blitzer's analysis of Barack Obama's speech addressing the Jeremiah Wright controversy. Rosen argues that Blitzer's interpretation, focusing solely on political strategy, misses the speech's deeper message urging a transcendence of divisive political discourse and a more nuanced understanding of race. Rosen contrasts Blitzer's shallow analysis with the insightful observations of Greg Sargent and Charles Murray, highlighting Obama's direct challenge to the media's role in perpetuating a spectacle-driven, race-focused narrative.
RECORD-00238.quote: It is so far above the standard we’re used to from our pols… rhetorically, but also in capturing a lot of nuance about race in America.
RECORD-00238.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00323.summary: Rosen critiques the prevailing notion of journalistic neutrality, arguing that it hinders effective political reporting and undermines democratic processes. It uses examples like Clark Hoyt's defense of the New York Times' neutrality, Josh Marshall's TPM's transparently liberal approach, and Walter Pincus' call for journalistic courage to illustrate the need for a more politically engaged and self-aware press. The piece emphasizes the importance of fairness over neutrality, advocating for transparency about reporters' political affiliations and a reevaluation of the power dynamics between the press and government, particularly addressing the legacy of controlled messaging started during the Reagan administration.
RECORD-00323.quote: “The biggest reason to go open kimono is that the present system does what journalism should never do: it perpetuates a lie.”
RECORD-00323.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00014.summary: The article analyzes instances where news organizations, particularly The New York Times and The Washington Post, engage in 'misguided contrarianism' by publishing provocative or seemingly iconoclastic pieces that ultimately serve to promote the paper's self-image rather than contribute meaningfully to public discourse. It critiques the pressure to 'find something' on all political candidates and the tendency to prioritize staff morale or economic concerns over journalistic integrity.
RECORD-00014.quote: The paper is not so much a paper anymore; it is itself a candidate.
RECORD-00014.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00012.summary: Jay Rosen questions the New York Times' decisions to investigate Obama's drug use, Hillary Clinton's marriage, and John McCain's lobbyist ties. He argues that each story went "weirdly wrong" and asks Romenesko readers for insights into what might have been the common factors behind these editorial choices during the vetting process of presidential candidates.
RECORD-00012.quote: Each was part of the “vetting” ritual in which the press imagines itself asking the hard questions of candidates who would be president. Each has a touch of the bizarre to it.
RECORD-00012.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00336.summary: Rosen is a distillation of a New York Times Q&A with readers regarding their explosive report on John McCain's involvement with lobbyist Vicki Iseman. The NYT defends its reporting choices, addressing concerns about anonymity, the inclusion of potentially unverified information about a romantic relationship, the timing of the story, and the potential impact on McCain's campaign. They maintain the story's accuracy and their commitment to thorough investigative journalism, despite the significant backlash.
RECORD-00336.quote: We publish stories when they’re ready. Period. No matter when we publish them people see dark motives.
RECORD-00336.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00343.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times' handling of a story suggesting John McCain had an affair. Rosen criticizes the Times' editors for lacking political awareness, failing to understand the potential consequences of their reporting, and clinging to journalistic codes that prevented them from recognizing the political realities of the situation. He argues that the Times' readers exhibited a more nuanced understanding of the political implications than the editors, highlighting a credibility gap between the newspaper and its audience.
RECORD-00343.quote: If a newspaper is going to suggest an improper sexual affair, whether editors think that is the central point or not, it owes readers more proof than The Times was able to provide.
RECORD-00343.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00694.summary: Rosen proposes a specific editorial assignment for the New York Times, arguing that the paper's journalism would improve if it approached certain stories with different methods and greater accountability.
RECORD-00694.quote: Rosen argues that the New York Times could produce better journalism by approaching certain stories with different methods and a stronger commitment to accountability, rather than defaulting to the conventions of detached, view-from-nowhere reporting.
RECORD-00694.author: Jay Rosen

CLIP-00007.summary: Article discusses the backlash against the New York Times for publishing a story based on anonymous sources regarding John McCain's alleged relationship with a lobbyist. Mentions Jay Rosen's commentary on the story on NYTPicker.com.
CLIP-00007.quote: The Times' reliance on anonymous sources in the McCain story generated backlash that overshadowed the reporting itself, illustrating how sourcing decisions can become the story.
CLIP-00007.author: Connecticut Post

RECORD-00358.summary: This blog post analyzes the New York Times's reporting on John McCain's alleged affair, questioning the timing of the story in relation to the paper's endorsement of McCain. Rosen raises concerns about the reliance on anonymous sources, the potential impact on the 2008 election, and the broader implications for media ethics and the relationship between the newsroom and editorial page. The piece also highlights the ensuing culture war and the Times's discomfort with defending its journalistic choices in the court of public opinion.
RECORD-00358.quote: For the New York Times, self-confidence on ethics poses its own risks, as well.
RECORD-00358.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00011.summary: Jay Rosen critiques horse race journalism, arguing that the campaign media operates as a 'herd of independent minds' lacking a central direction or capacity to learn from mistakes. This mindlessness results in superficial coverage focused on predicting outcomes rather than understanding the stakes, leading to inaccurate narratives and a failure to inform the public effectively.
RECORD-00011.quote: Campaign reporters tend to be massively other-directed. The reality-check is what the rest of the press is doing.
RECORD-00011.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00691.summary: An examination of the OffTheBus/NewsTrust collaboration to crowdsource quality political coverage, describing a test of filtering the best citizen journalism to the front page during the 2008 campaign.
RECORD-00691.quote: The OffTheBus/NewsTrust collaboration tested whether crowdsourced filters could surface the best citizen journalism to a front page during the 2008 campaign, treating quality political coverage as something readers could help identify, not just consume.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00691.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00271.summary: Rosen analyzes the contrasting views of the conservative elite and the conservative base regarding the media. While the base often perceives the press as monolithic, liberal, and against the Bush administration, key figures like Karl Rove and Dan Bartlett, having gained insider experience, recognize a more nuanced reality. They acknowledge the press's inherent desire for compelling stories and its oppositional stance towards power, irrespective of party affiliation. This divergence highlights a strategic utilization of the base's perception of media bias to serve political goals, while insiders operate with a more pragmatic understanding of journalistic motivations.
RECORD-00271.quote: The press is generally liberal, he argued, but “I think it’s less liberal than it is oppositional.”
RECORD-00271.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00295.summary: Jay Rosen argues that Scott McClellan's role as White House press secretary under George W. Bush was not simply to disseminate information, but to actively frustrate and belittle the press, hindering genuine communication and increasing the opacity of the executive branch. McClellan's actions, Rosen contends, were part of a broader strategy by the Bush administration to reduce constraints on presidential power and limit accountability through strategic non-communication, rather than outright lying or traditional spin.
RECORD-00295.quote: McClellan’s specialty was not lying, or the traditional art of spin, but what I have called “strategic non-communication.” Lying we understand; spin we have to come to grasp. Non-communication we still do not appreciate. Its purpose is to make executive power less legible.
RECORD-00295.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00383.summary: Jay Rosen announces the launch of Beatblogging.org, a project involving 13 news organizations and their reporters who will experiment with integrating social networks into their beat reporting.  The goal is to explore whether a collaborative, pro-am approach to journalism, using social networks to connect with experts and the public, can improve the quality and reach of beat reporting.  The project will run for a year, with participating organizations including the Houston Chronicle, Star-Ledger, Wired.com, and others, each focusing on a different beat.
RECORD-00383.quote: The reporter was a gatekeeper before only the expertise he chose would make it to the public in print. But now the role of the reporter can and should be different: as a moderator, vetter, enabler, encourager.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00383.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00453.summary: Rosen analyzes the implosion of Wide Open, a political blog run by the Cleveland Plain Dealer.  The blog's demise stemmed from a contributor's political donation to an opponent of a Congressman, leading to the newspaper's decision to sever ties with the contributor, and ultimately, the shutdown of the blog. Rosen critiques the newspaper's handling of the situation, arguing that prioritizing traditional journalistic ethics over transparency exacerbated the crisis and reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the blogosphere's dynamics.  Rosen advocates for transparency as a more suitable approach for online opinion pieces.
RECORD-00453.quote: Transparency is not some new media buzzword but an alternative means of generating trust.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00453.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00354.summary: Rosen proposes an experiment to improve beat reporting by integrating social networks. Rosen seeks 12 beat reporters to create online communities around their beats, allowing for collaboration with experts and stakeholders outside the newsroom. The goal is to enhance reporting quality and explore new models for journalistic practice in the digital age using tools like blogs, wikis, and forums.
RECORD-00354.quote: Maybe a beat reporter could do a way better job if there was a live social network connected to the beat, made up of people who know the territory the beat covers, and want the reporting on that beat to be better.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00354.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00321.summary: Rosen outlines a model for successful online news organizations, focusing on features like high-quality aggregation, blogging platforms, original reporting with amateur and professional collaborations, beat blogging, comprehensive features, interactive forums, data visualization, community publishing, reverse publishing, crowdsourcing, breaking news coverage, geo-tagged information, search-optimized content, and comprehensive topic pages. Rosen presents this as a list of coordinates, not a rigid formula, for the future of online news.
RECORD-00321.quote: Like my coordinates for distributed journalism, these are the coordinates I see for the emerging model of a successful online news organization.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00321.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00185.summary: Rosen reflects on the lessons learned from Assignment Zero, a collaborative journalism project with Wired.com that aimed to explore the potential of pro-am journalism. Rosen analyzes the challenges and successes of the project, highlighting the importance of proper division of labor, understanding contributors' motivations, managing coordination costs, and ensuring clear connections between individual contributions and the overall narrative. Key takeaways include the need for appropriately sized tasks, inspiring participation rather than commanding it, and leveraging existing online communities for efficient distributed reporting.
RECORD-00185.quote: Newsrooms developed as monasteries not because reporters were anointed (though many believe they were and are) but because there wasn’t really any frictionless way to include the public in the reporting enterprise. Now there is.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00185.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00391.summary: Rosen analyzes Dan Rather's $70 million lawsuit against CBS, focusing on the theatricality of the event and its reflection of Rather's personality and career.  Rosen explores Rather's self-perception as a hard-news investigative reporter despite his role as a prominent anchor, examining his motivations for the lawsuit as a final attempt to reclaim his journalistic integrity and expose alleged collusion between CBS and the Bush administration in the Killian memo controversy.  The piece also considers broader implications regarding the role of anchors, the accountability of mainstream media versus bloggers, and the changing landscape of journalism.
RECORD-00391.quote: Rather told King he “would like the legacy of this lawsuit to be not that I made tons of money out of it, but that we kept the little flame, the flickering flame of hard-nose investigative reporting alive.”
RECORD-00391.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00690.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times's decision to shut down TimesSelect, framing it as a verdict by "the court of the web" against paywalling opinion content, and what it means for the future of newspaper business models.
RECORD-00690.quote: The New York Times's decision to shut down TimesSelect was a verdict by 'the court of the web' against paywalling opinion content — a ruling that exposed the limits of newspaper subscription models in an era of open information.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00690.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00454.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times' decision to shut down TimesSelect, its paywalled content section.  Rosen argues that the failure of TimesSelect demonstrates the futility of charging for online content in the face of the open web's link-based economy and the power of search engine optimization.  The Times' shift towards an open model, embracing search engine traffic and blogosphere participation, is presented as a strategic necessity for long-term success and revenue generation through advertising tied to search.
RECORD-00454.quote: The professional premium is better located there.
RECORD-00454.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00265.summary: Rosen is a blog post presenting a dialogue between Jay Rosen and a White House correspondent (“Hack”) regarding the role and limitations of the White House press corps. The correspondent challenges Rosen’s criticism of the corps’ coverage of the President’s trip to Iraq, arguing that the “body watch” – the constant monitoring of the President for safety reasons – necessitates their presence, even in potentially propagandistic settings. The discussion expands to explore the overreliance on the White House for news, the influence of access and “insider” information, and the need for a more balanced approach incorporating outside perspectives.
RECORD-00265.quote: What we are responsible for is making sure that, if he collapses, or is shot at, we are in a position to get that information to your viewers/listeners/readers.
RECORD-00265.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00261.summary: Rosen analyzes the failure of the press to adequately cover the Bush administration's expansion of executive power. It highlights Charlie Savage's work in uncovering the administration's agenda of concentrating unchecked power in the White House, arguing that this 'master narrative' was crucial for understanding various seemingly disparate events. Rosen criticizes the press for failing to connect these events and for accepting a superficial understanding of the Bush administration's political strategy. He emphasizes the long-term consequences of this unchecked expansion of presidential power, regardless of future administrations' actions.
RECORD-00261.quote: The administration, from its very beginning, had set out to set precedents and take actions that would permanently expand presidential power for the long-term, even when such tactics brought them extra short-term difficulties.
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes
RECORD-00261.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00572.summary: Rosen analyzes the failure of the Washington press corps to adequately cover the Bush administration, arguing that their adherence to established methods and a cyclical view of politics left them unprepared for the administration's radicalism.  Rosen critiques the press's deference to figures like Karl Rove, attributing it not solely to personal admiration but also to a lack of imagination and preparedness for unconventional political tactics.  The article uses the examples of the Iraq War coverage and the underreporting of Dick Cheney's power to illustrate the shortcomings of the press's approach.
RECORD-00572.quote: The media virtually never takes seriously any administration lawbreaking and corruption scandals because the people at the center of those scandals are those whom they deeply admire.
RECORD-00572.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00390.summary: Rosen is a response to Michael Skube's opinion piece in the Los Angeles Times criticizing blogs' journalistic value.  Rosen challenges Skube's claims by providing numerous examples of blogs engaging in thorough fact-finding and investigative reporting. He argues that the traditional journalistic gatekeeping system is being challenged by the rise of citizen journalism and that the act of reporting is inherently democratic and not limited to professionally trained journalists.
RECORD-00390.quote: If you have a blog, you never know when you might be called on to also be a journalist.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00390.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00803.summary: Rosen responds to Michael Skube's LA Times op-ed dismissing blogs as 'noise that fits,' arguing that bloggers like Joshua Micah Marshall do substantive investigative journalism — and noting that Skube wrote about blogs without having read them.
RECORD-00803.quote: Rosen critiques Michael Skube's dismissive opinion piece about blogs and their role in journalism, arguing bloggers do real investigative and verification work.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00803.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00218.summary: This text is a draft of a response by Jay Rosen to Michael Skube's critique of blogs. Rosen compiles a list of examples showcasing various instances of citizen journalism and blog-based investigative reporting to counter Skube's arguments. The examples highlight blogs' contributions to newsgathering and information dissemination across diverse fields, including politics, technology, and consumer affairs, demonstrating their capacity for in-depth investigations and breaking news.
RECORD-00218.quote: Pet owners frustrated with the limitations of the news media self-organize into a national network of sites and share news about tainted foods that may have killed thousands of pets across the country.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00218.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00473.summary: This is a short, angry blog post directed at an unnamed journalist.  Rosen accuses the journalist of being an embarrassment to the profession, calls for their resignation, criticizes their reporting (specifically citing the Los Angeles Times and Walter Reed Army Medical Center coverage), and implies a lack of commitment to learning and reporting.
RECORD-00473.quote: You’re an embarrassment to my profession, to the university where you teach, and to the craft of reporting you claim to defend.
RECORD-00473.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00316.summary: Rosen argues that the vulnerability of the American press to manipulation by figures like Karl Rove stems from an unspoken ideology of 'savviness' within journalism. Rosen contends that journalists prioritize shrewdness and winning, even at the expense of honesty, fairness, and ethical considerations. He uses Karl Rove's career and the press's coverage of his resignation as examples to illustrate how this prioritization of savviness allowed Rove to exploit and manipulate the media.
RECORD-00316.quote: Savviness—that quality of being shrewd, practical, well-informed, perceptive, ironic, “with it,” and unsentimental in all things political—is, in a sense, their professional religion.
RECORD-00316.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00484.summary: Rosen discusses the evolving relationship between mainstream media and the blogosphere in 2007, focusing on political journalism.  Mainstream journalists are increasingly acknowledging the value of blogosphere input, recognizing that readers often possess more knowledge than reporters. However, the piece also critiques the tendency of some journalists to prioritize appearing politically neutral over truthful reporting, leading to a superficial and often misleading approach to news coverage.  Rosen uses examples from YearlyKos and various journalists' comments to illustrate how the pressure to avoid partisan labels can compromise journalistic integrity.
RECORD-00484.quote: Simply put, news is no longer a one-way process. It is now much more of a conversation between journalist and reader.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00484.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00558.summary: Rosen reflects on the 2007 Yearly Kos convention, highlighting the growing influence of online political blogging and its impact on the relationship between politicians, the press, and the public.  Rosen emphasizes the role of Daily Kos and its community in shaping political discourse, arguing that its participatory nature prioritizes argument and engagement over purely informational reporting, a contrast to traditional journalism's approach.  Rosen notes the acknowledgment from journalists like Matt Bai of the press's failures, particularly during the Iraq War, and the evolving relationship between bloggers and traditional journalists.
RECORD-00558.quote: We the press failed you, the people whom Bush actively misled. We failed by not stopping him.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00558.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00373.summary: This FAQ post provides guidance to contributors of OffTheBus, a collaborative project between Huffington Post and New Assignment, on how to create effective blog posts for a campaign journalism platform. It emphasizes the importance of providing original information, conducting original reporting, and filling gaps in existing news coverage rather than simply offering opinion or commentary. Rosen's post offers examples of successful posts and suggests developing a specific beat for consistent contributions.
RECORD-00373.quote: One of the keys to a successful “norg” — and saving the endangered jobs of American journalists like me — will be to stop talking down to or even insulting our so-called “audience” of readers — but forming a working partnership with everyday citizens who care about good journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00373.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00689.summary: A complete transcript and analysis of all citizen-submitted questions from the CNN/YouTube Democratic presidential debate in Charleston, SC, examining what this format revealed about the gap between what citizens and journalists consider important.
RECORD-00689.quote: The gap between the questions citizens chose to submit and the questions professional journalists would have asked reveals a persistent disconnect between press values and public concerns.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00689.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00305.summary: This Q&A discusses the lessons learned from Assignment Zero, a crowdsourced journalism project, and how those lessons are being applied to OffTheBus, a new open platform campaign news bureau. Key takeaways include the importance of clear task assignments, aligning tasks with contributors' motivations, and the limitations of a purely “gift economy” model for news. The discussion also touches upon the nature of political journalism and the challenges of synthesizing large amounts of crowdsourced material.
RECORD-00305.quote: People will contribute only because they want to, because the work stirs a passion they have, or is inherently interesting or they find the community of people, a great group of people and everything starts from there, not from “what needs to be done,” but the motivations and interests of the people joining the project.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00305.author: Jay Rosen and Leonard Witt

RECORD-00688.summary: A companion piece to the OffTheBus launch, defining the project's editorial mission — "Inquire. Discover. Inform Others." — and articulating what citizen journalism at its best should look like.
RECORD-00688.quote: Citizen journalism at its best follows a simple but demanding mandate: inquire into what matters, discover what's actually true, and inform others clearly and honestly.
RECORD-00688.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00687.summary: Rosen publishes editorial guidelines for OffTheBus, the citizen journalism project he co-founded with Arianna Huffington for the 2008 presidential campaign, establishing standards for volunteer bloggers.
RECORD-00687.quote: To earn the trust of readers, citizen journalists must hold themselves to the same standards of accuracy, transparency, and fairness that define credible reporting at any level.
RECORD-00687.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00409.summary: This article features an interview with James Surowiecki, author of "The Wisdom of Crowds."  The conversation explores the implications of crowdsourcing and online collaboration, particularly regarding the aggregation of opinions to form collective judgment.  Surowiecki distinguishes between the rise of individual bloggers and the true wisdom of crowds, emphasizing the need for mechanisms to aggregate diverse opinions effectively.  The discussion also touches upon the digital divide, the role of past experiences in collective wisdom, the potential for online participation to translate into real-world activism, and the application of the wisdom of crowds to address complex issues like global warming.  Finally, Surowiecki reflects on his career transition from book critic to business columnist, highlighting the opportunities presented by the internet and the ongoing public interest in business and economics.
RECORD-00409.quote: You only get real collective wisdom when you have some way of aggregating lots of different individual opinions to produce a collective judgment.
RECORD-00409.author: Emily Gordon

RECORD-00177.summary: Rosen critiques Mother Jones magazine's coverage of "Politics 2.0," arguing that their framing of the topic as a simple "it'll change everything/it'll change nothing" dichotomy is simplistic and misses the nuances of the impact of the internet on politics. Rosen contends that Mother Jones relies on tired journalistic tropes instead of offering a thoughtful analysis, ignoring insightful observations from their own interviewees. He highlights the missed opportunity to explore the generational conflict within political campaigns regarding internet usage and the evolving role of gatekeepers in the digital age.
RECORD-00177.quote: What they have accomplished in just a few years is astonishing. Already, the netroots are the most significant mass movement in U.S. politics since the rise of the Christian right more than two decades ago. And, by all appearances, they are far from finished with their task: recreating the Democratic Party in the image of the conservative machine they have set out to destroy.
RECORD-00177.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00536.summary: Rosen announces the launch of OffTheBus.Net, a collaborative campaign journalism project spearheaded by Jay Rosen, Arianna Huffington, and the Huffington Post.  The project aims to create a more open and participatory approach to covering political campaigns, utilizing a blogging platform where volunteers can contribute.  While acknowledging potential biases due to the project's origins within a liberal-leaning online environment, the authors emphasize a commitment to accuracy and quality across all contributions. The article also discusses the challenges and potential benefits of this open, participatory model of journalism, contrasting it with traditional newsroom structures.
RECORD-00536.quote: They both understand that the falling costs for like-minded people to find each other, share information and collaborate on good works (as well as works of evil….) probably means we can do new and exciting things in political journalism, but it is still very hard to do those things because our knowledge of how to organize scattered people with limited time and definite interest is still primitive.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00536.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00472.summary: Rosen critiques the prevalent "horse race" narrative in political campaign reporting, arguing that it prioritizes who's winning over substantive policy discussions.  Rosen proposes an "Idea Race" alternative, where candidates are ranked based on their policy proposals and engagement with key issues. This approach aims to shift the focus from mere electability to the merits of different policy platforms and fosters a more informed public discourse. The piece also touches upon the challenges of changing ingrained journalistic practices and the potential biases in media coverage.
RECORD-00472.quote: Most people who pay attention to politics know that candidates who cannot win are safely ignored by the press until they threaten to affect the outcome.
RECORD-00472.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00463.summary: Rosen discusses the tension between veteran journalists and the emerging digital media landscape.  Veteran journalists, exemplified by Neil Henry's critique of Google's role in the decline of traditional news, express resentment towards search engines and online platforms for profiting from journalistic content without sufficient reciprocal support.  Younger journalists and commentators, however, argue that the problem lies not with technology but with the outdated business models of traditional media. The piece highlights the generational divide, contrasting the anxieties of older journalists with the more optimistic adaptation of younger ones to the digital world.
RECORD-00463.quote: Technology isnt destroying journalism. Its simply destroying the business that subsidized journalism.
RECORD-00463.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00483.summary: This article critiques the American press's failure to maintain independence and accurately report on significant events, particularly the Iraq War.  The authors argue that the press's reliance on official sources, pursuit of insider politics, and adherence to a flawed notion of objectivity led to complicity in the administration's manipulation of the news.  They highlight instances where the press missed or downplayed crucial information, contributing to public misinformation and a lack of critical scrutiny of government actions. The authors suggest that the press's ingrained dependence on government for legitimacy prevents it from effectively challenging power, even when recognizing its own failings.
RECORD-00483.quote: Legions of critics and off-duty journalists are searching for answers to why it is so difficult to be independent and get stories straight. Why is it so hard to resist the ever-present spin of those in power?
RECORD-00483.author: W. Lance Bennett, Regina G. Lawrence, and Steven Livingston

RECORD-00686.summary: A response to Howard Kurtz's column about the decline of the traditional media interview, examining how the internet and blogging have changed the power dynamics between journalists and their subjects.
RECORD-00686.quote: The internet and blogging have shifted the power dynamics between journalists and their subjects, putting the traditional media interview — and the journalists who conduct it — under new forms of pressure.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00686.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00267.summary: Rosen is a transcript of an email interview between Jay Rosen and Howard Kurtz, discussing the changing nature of the interview in the context of the rise of the internet and citizen journalism. Rosen argues that the traditional interview is not obsolete, but the balance of power has shifted due to sources having more direct access to audiences. He discusses his experiences with interviews, the limitations of soundbites, and the challenges of collaborative journalism projects like Assignment Zero and Off the Bus, which aim to incorporate citizen contributors into news coverage.
RECORD-00267.quote: What’s missing is any openness to the idea that an interview can be truly dialogic - that the interviewer has as much to learn as the interviewee.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00267.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00554.summary: Rosen presents an interview with Susan Gardner of Daily Kos about crowdsourced journalism.  Gardner discusses the potential of crowdsourcing for analyzing large datasets (like proposed legislation or email dumps), the motivations of contributors (a sense of civic duty and frustration with mainstream media), and the challenges of managing crowdsourced projects (coordination, avoiding excessive research tangents, and defining success).  She highlights the importance of clear roles, strong collaborative software, and a balance between researchers and writers in successful projects.  The interview is presented as a work-in-progress, soliciting further questions and input from readers.
RECORD-00554.quote: I think its also a revival of the notion of participatory democracy. Those who are gifted with analysis, research and interpretive skills feel they’re giving something back to the country by exposing corruption.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00554.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00268.summary: Rosen presents a correspondence between Jay Rosen and Neil Lewis of the New York Times. Lewis objects to Rosen's criticism of a colleague's interview practices, arguing that editing and condensing are inherent to journalism. Rosen clarifies his criticism, focusing not on the editing itself but on the reporter's framing of a discussion about the White House Correspondents' Dinner within a misleading 'bloggers vs. journalists' narrative. Rosen contends that this framing obscures a larger issue: the failure of the press to adequately confront its relationship with the Bush administration and its role in the Iraq War.
RECORD-00268.quote: The failure of much of the American press to uncover — and provide some prominence to — the private doubts and even the public case against the war was, in my view, it’s most egregious failure in my 50 years in journalism.
RECORD-00268.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00324.summary: Rosen details the progress and challenges of Assignment Zero, a collaborative journalism project exploring crowdsourcing and peer production. The project, initially focused on a broad investigation of wisdom-of-the-crowd efforts, shifted to a more focused approach involving five key topics and an "Interview Week" to gather information from key figures. The project utilized a Creative Commons license, emphasizing transparency and open collaboration. Challenges included creating a user-friendly platform for contributors and initially selecting a complex first story. Despite setbacks, the project aimed to produce five feature stories and numerous Q&As for Wired.com, with support from the Online News Association.
RECORD-00324.quote: Whether Assignment Zero worked or not is ultimately in the journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00324.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00192.summary: Rosen critiques the White House Correspondents' Dinner, arguing that it symbolizes the failure of the press to hold power accountable, particularly during the Bush administration. Rosen discusses the changing relationship between the press and the White House, noting the Bush administration's attempts to marginalize and discredit the press. Rosen also reflects on his own experiences being interviewed for news stories, highlighting the power dynamics between reporters and sources and the limitations of traditional journalistic interviews in the age of blogging.
RECORD-00192.quote: In our democracy, the people who represent the public stood for election… I don’t believe you have a check-and-balance function.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00192.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00567.summary: This article discusses the necessary changes in newsroom leadership, culture, and training for newspapers to survive in the digital age.  It highlights the shift from autocratic management styles to collaborative leadership, emphasizing the need for communication, coaching, and risk-taking. The authors also detail the importance of transitioning from defensive newsroom cultures to adaptive ones that foster creativity and initiative, suggesting strategies such as increased training and staff-level decision-making.
RECORD-00567.quote: The future of news will belong to those who build it.
RECORD-00567.author: Michele McLellan and Tim Porter

RECORD-00335.summary: Jay Rosen and Arianna Huffington announce a joint venture in campaign journalism, involving a large network of contributors covering various presidential candidates. The project, housed on NewAssignment.Net and affiliated with the Huffington Post, aims to provide diverse perspectives on the campaign beyond traditional media's limitations, utilizing a ‘pro-am’ model with volunteer contributors and a Creative Commons license. While the initiative embraces the potential of many voices, concerns are raised about the potential for the project to still reflect dominant perspectives rather than genuinely diverse ones.
RECORD-00335.quote: So instead of one well-placed reporter trailing John Edwards wherever he goes (which is one way of doing it) some 40 or 50 differently-placed people tracking different parts of the Edwards campaign, all with peculiar beats and personal blogs linked together by virtue of having a common editor and a page through which the best and most original stuff filters out to the greater readership of the Web, especially via the Huffington Post.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00335.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00386.summary: Rosen is a call to action, recruiting journalists and other skilled individuals to volunteer for Assignment Zero, a crowdsourced journalism project.  The project aims to collaboratively report on the spread of crowdsourcing and peer production methods, breaking down a large story into manageable parts for a team of professional and amateur contributors.  Rosen highlights the need for editors, reporters, web-savvy journalists, organizers, and developers to help manage the project's complexity and scale, emphasizing the innovative, pro-am model of journalism.
RECORD-00386.quote: Journalism by the many, edited by a few, requires great efficiency and strong systems.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00386.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00397.summary: Rosen announces Assignment Zero, a collaborative journalism project exploring the potential of crowdsourcing and peer production in newsgathering.  The project aims to investigate the spread of crowdsourcing, using a pro-am model involving professional journalists and citizen journalists working together to report on a topic at a scale beyond the capabilities of a traditional newsroom.  The initiative highlights the shift in the relationship between journalists and audiences, leveraging the informational strengths of the 'people formerly known as the audience' and embracing radical transparency.
RECORD-00397.quote: Our hope is that a team of professionals, working with scores of citizen journalists, is capable of completing an investigative project of far greater scope than a team of two or three professionals ever could.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00397.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00551.summary: Rosen analyzes Firedoglake's coverage of the Scooter Libby trial, arguing that its live-blogging, driven by a committed community and a lack of official coverage, produced superior reporting to that of mainstream media.  Rosen contrasts the established journalistic norms with Firedoglake's success, highlighting the changing media landscape and the potential of online communities to generate reliable and impactful news coverage.
RECORD-00551.quote: Blogging allows us to go direct with our knowledge, experience and insights, without waiting for a reporter to ask us what we think.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00551.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00523.summary: Rosen analyzes the conservative backlash against the mainstream media, particularly focusing on the Iraq War.  It argues that the distrust of the mainstream media among conservatives, fueled by partisan loyalty to President Bush and a desire to discredit perceived liberal bias, led to a detachment from reality regarding the situation in Iraq.  Rosen highlights how this rejection of empirical evidence hampered effective policy and contributed to the war's failure, contrasting the actions of conservatives with the more realistic assessment offered by some conservative voices like Rich Lowry, who acknowledged the mainstream media's accuracy in reporting on the war's dire conditions. The article uses the Jamil Hussein controversy as a case study to illustrate these broader points about political polarization and the role of media.
RECORD-00523.quote: “Realism is essential in any war, and it is impossible without an ability to assimilate bad news, even bad news that comes from distasteful sources.”
RECORD-00523.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00400.summary: Rosen discusses the launch of Placeblogger.com, a website designed to connect and promote hyperlocal blogs.  Rosen highlights the significance of placeblogs as a form of community-based journalism, emphasizing their focus on lived experience and local news beyond the scope of traditional media.  The article also features commentary from various individuals in the blogosphere and traditional media, discussing the potential impact of placeblogs on the future of journalism and the changing media landscape.
RECORD-00400.quote: Placeblogs represent the lived experience of a place; newspapers reflect the tiny slice of that experience that is news.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00400.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00549.summary: Rosen analyzes Ron Suskind's article "Without a Doubt," focusing on the Bush administration's rejection of "reality-based community" decision-making.  Rosen argues that the Bush administration prioritized action over evidence-based policy, actively shaping reality through its actions and suppressing dissenting voices.  He contrasts this approach with traditional policymaking and discusses the implications for the press and the setting of public narratives about events like the Iraq War.
RECORD-00549.quote: We’re an empire now, and when we act, we create our own reality. And while you’re studying that reality — judiciously, as you will — we’ll act again, creating other new realities, which you can study too, and that’s how things will sort out.
RECORD-00549.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00350.summary: GateHouse Media, a newspaper conglomerate, is adopting Creative Commons licenses for nearly all its Massachusetts newspapers and TownOnline sites, a move toward greater openness on the web. This decision, though using a restrictive non-commercial license, is significant as few major media outlets have embraced CC licensing. The company is also incorporating user-generated content and open-source software (Zope) into its platforms, potentially impacting newsroom jobs but also presenting opportunities for innovation and revenue generation through increased online traffic and potential software sales. The article discusses the implications of this open approach, including potential challenges and the intriguing reception from investors who see it as an internet-style business model.
RECORD-00350.quote: For a major publisher with significant numbers of people reading to be doing this is great.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00350.author: Lisa Williams

RECORD-00424.summary: This is a Q&A with John Harris and Jim VandeHei, who left the Washington Post to start a new “multi-platform” political news operation.  The conversation centers on their reasons for leaving, their vision for a new kind of political journalism that emphasizes individual journalist signatures, in-depth reporting beyond the “front story,”  a more conversational and transparent style, and a multi-platform approach leveraging web and broadcast partnerships. They aim to fill a perceived niche in political news by providing insightful context and behind-the-scenes reporting that other outlets are not consistently delivering.
RECORD-00424.quote: We believe that for people who want this type of stability, journalism is not going to remain an attractive profession for much longer. But people who adapt will thrive and end up having more fun than in the old days.
RECORD-00424.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00481.summary: Rosen analyzes the departure of John Harris and Jim VandeHei from the Washington Post to launch a new multi-platform political news operation with Allbritton Communications.  Rosen questions the novelty of their proclaimed "next generation" approach, which emphasizes transparency and interactivity but appears to rely on traditional journalistic practices and insider access.  The core innovation seems to be a willingness to break established norms regarding source disclosure and the unspoken agreements within political reporting.
RECORD-00481.quote: There’s little question we’re in the midst of a period of profound change, and the moves by Harris and VandeHei are a fascinating reminder of that fact.
RECORD-00481.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00276.summary: This interview between Jay Rosen and John McQuaid discusses the evolving role of technology and citizen participation in investigative journalism. McQuaid highlights the potential of online communities and networks for collaborative reporting, enabling journalists to access diverse perspectives and expertise. Rosen and McQuaid debate the limitations of traditional “he said, she said” journalism and advocate for more assertive investigative reporting that draws conclusions and challenges established narratives, even acknowledging the potential backlash from ideologically committed groups. The discussion centers on the need for innovative reporting techniques to maintain public confidence and deliver impactful, explanatory journalism in a rapidly changing media landscape.
RECORD-00276.quote: Journalists are in the business of assembling and refining knowledge — not just facts, but ideas — and we need allies of all stripes.
RECORD-00276.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00448.summary: Rosen is an interview with John McQuaid, a Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist who left the Times-Picayune due to cost-cutting and the changing landscape of journalism.  McQuaid discusses his transition to online investigative journalism, reflecting on the limitations of traditional newspaper models and the potential of the web for in-depth reporting. He highlights the shift in access to information, the changing role of the reader, and the challenges and opportunities of adapting investigative journalism to the dynamic nature of the internet.
RECORD-00448.quote: Newspaper journalists watched the revolution unfold on their desktops along with everyone else, and rejoiced. But, of course, without knowing it, we were also watching our own relevancy decline.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00448.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00205.summary: Rosen discusses the Polling Place Photo Project (PPPP), an open-source initiative aiming to document the American voting experience through citizen-generated photographs. The project, a collaboration between AIGA, Design Observer, and NewAssignment.Net, seeks to improve the accuracy and understanding of the voting process by supplementing traditional media coverage with firsthand visual accounts. It also serves as a test case for the feasibility and ergonomics of large-scale, volunteer-based, open-source data collection and social network reporting.
RECORD-00205.quote: The project’s goal, according to its designer and prime mover William Drenttel, is “an archive of photographs that captures the richness and complexity of voting in America.” A second aim is to “encourage research into how voting happens and how voting can be made easier, clearer, less confusing, more reliable.”
